messages.content: The kitchen tap in our flat has gone weak over the last month, but the bathroom taps and shower are fine. What should I look at first?

Because only one outlet is affected, the supply to the house is almost certainly fine — the restriction is local to that tap or its feed. Most likely causes, in order: (1) a clogged aerator — the mesh screen at the spout traps grit and scale and is the single commonest cause of a single tap fading gradually; (2) a partially blocked or kinked flexible connector under the sink; (3) a failing cartridge or washer inside the tap itself.

Cheapest discriminating check: unscrew the aerator by hand or with a cloth-wrapped wrench, rinse out the debris, and run the tap without it. If the flow is strong bare, the aerator was the whole problem — clean or replace it for pennies. If flow is still weak with the aerator off, shut the tap's isolation valve, disconnect the flexible hose, and point it into a bucket while briefly opening the valve: strong flow there means the blockage is inside the tap (cartridge swap, a DIY job with the water off); weak flow means the restriction is upstream in that branch.

Decision point: all of this is DIY-safe with the stopcock known and no pipes cut. Call a plumber only if the weak flow turns out to be in fixed pipework or the isolation valve itself leaks when touched.
Every tap in the house has lost pressure at the same time, and it happened suddenly yesterday. The neighbours say theirs is fine. Where do I start?

Whole-house, sudden, and neighbours unaffected points at something between the street main and your taps, or one valve event inside the house. Likely causes in order: (1) the main stopcock or a gate valve was knocked or partially closed — check whether anyone worked near it, and whether a gate valve's spindle has dropped (old gate valves can close themselves as the washer perishes); (2) a failed pressure-reducing valve if your supply runs through one; (3) a leak on your service pipe — a burst underground feed loses pressure everywhere at once; (4) a frozen section in cold weather.

Discriminating checks, cheapest first: fully open the main stopcock and re-test. Then read the water meter with every tap off — if the dial still creeps, water is escaping somewhere, which promotes the leak theory to first place; walk the garden and driveway looking for a boggy patch or greener strip. If the meter is still and the stopcock is open, the PRV or a failed valve is left.

Decision point: stopcock and meter checks are yours. A leaking service pipe, a seized stopcock, or PRV replacement is a plumber's job — excavation and work on the supply side are not safe DIY.
Our toilet cistern refills a little every twenty minutes or so even when nobody has flushed, and sometimes we hear a faint hiss. What's going on?

That pattern — periodic phantom refills plus a hiss — is the classic signature of a slow leak from the cistern into the bowl, with the fill valve topping up the lost water. Two suspects: (1) the flush valve seal (flapper or drop-valve washer) is perished, gritty, or warped, letting water seep past it into the bowl — by far the most likely; (2) the fill valve itself is weeping or set so the waterline sits above the overflow.

Discriminating check, free and decisive: put a few drops of food colouring in the cistern, don't flush, and wait 20 minutes. Colour appearing in the bowl proves the flush seal is leaking. If the bowl stays clear but the level still drops, watch the overflow pipe — water trickling down it means the fill valve is overfilling instead.

Decision point: both fixes are DIY-friendly with the cistern's isolation valve closed — a replacement flapper or seal costs very little and fits in minutes. Call a plumber only if the cistern has no isolator and the main stopcock won't shut, or the close-coupled bolts are corroded solid.
The bathroom basin drains more and more slowly, and now it gurgles when the bath empties. The kitchen sink drains fine. How do I pin down where the blockage is?

Two clues locate it: the basin is slow, and it gurgles when a different fixture (the bath) discharges. Gurgling means air is being pushed or pulled through the basin trap because the shared branch is restricted — so the blockage is most likely in the pipework the basin and bath share, downstream of where they join, not in the basin trap alone. Causes in order: (1) a hair-and-soap mat in the shared branch, usually at a bend or a shallow fall; (2) a partial blockage in the basin trap itself (would not explain the gurgling); (3) a venting problem, less likely if this developed gradually.

Discriminating checks: first remove and clean the basin trap into a bucket — cheap and rules suspect 2 in or out. If the trap is clean and the basin still drains slowly with the trap off (run water carefully into the open pipe), the restriction is in the wall/floor branch: a hand-crank drain auger fed into the open waste is the next step.

Decision point: trap cleaning and a hand auger are safe DIY. Stop and call a plumber if the auger meets a hard obstruction it can't pass, if sewage backs up into the bath, or if the slow drain is on the ground floor with the toilet also sluggish — that pattern suggests the main drain, which is a jetting/rod job.
We get a loud bang in the pipes every time the washing machine finishes filling. It only started after we had a new, faster washing machine installed. Should I worry?

That bang is water hammer: a fast-closing solenoid valve stops moving water almost instantly, and the pressure wave slams back through the pipework. The new machine is the trigger because its valves snap shut faster than the old one's. Causes and contributors in order: (1) the quick-closing valve itself, with no arrestor fitted; (2) high static water pressure, which makes any hammer worse; (3) loose or unclipped pipe runs that bang against joists as they jump.

Discriminating checks: does the bang happen with any other single fast shut-off — a quarter-turn tap snapped closed? If only the machine triggers it, it's the valve speed. Measure static pressure at an outside tap with a cheap gauge if you have one: above about 3.5-4 bar at rest makes hammer far more likely and points to fitting a pressure-reducing valve as part of the cure.

Fix path (DIY-safe): fit a washing-machine water-hammer arrestor on the machine's supply tee — it screws on by hand — and clip any loose pipe runs you can reach. Worry level: repeated hammer loosens joints over years, so treat it, but it's not an emergency. Call a plumber if you find weeping joints already, or if pressure is high and there's no PRV — that install involves cutting into the supply.
There's a slow drip from the compression joint under my bathroom sink, maybe a drip every few seconds onto the cabinet floor. Can I fix this myself?

A slow drip at a compression joint is one of the most DIY-able plumbing faults, but diagnose before tightening: the drip comes from either (1) a slightly loose compression nut, (2) a damaged or mis-seated olive (the brass ring that bites the pipe), or (3) a hairline crack in the pipe or fitting body, which no amount of tightening will cure.

Discriminating check: dry the joint completely with tissue, then wrap a fresh strip of tissue around it and watch where the wet spot appears first. Wet at the nut threads points to the olive seal; wet on the pipe or fitting body points to a crack.

Fix: shut off the isolator (or drain down), then try a quarter-turn of extra tightness on the nut first — often enough. If it still weeps, undo the joint, inspect the olive: if it's scored or the pipe is dented under it, cut back to clean pipe and fit a new olive and nut. Decision point: all fine as DIY with the water isolated. Call a plumber if there's no way to isolate that feed, if the pipe is lead or badly corroded, or if the 'drip' turns out to be tracking down from the tap tail above — that changes the job entirely.
Our hot water pressure is much weaker than the cold at every tap, and the hot also takes longer than it used to to arrive. We have a combi boiler. What are the likely causes?

Weak hot everywhere with cold unaffected means the restriction is in the hot path: from the boiler's inlet, through its heat exchanger, or in the hot distribution. With a combi, likely causes in order: (1) a scaled or debris-clogged plate heat exchanger or inlet filter — combis throttle hot flow hard when the plate scales up, and the longer wait fits a reduced flow rate rather than a longer pipe run; (2) a partially closed isolation valve on the boiler's cold inlet; (3) a failing flow sensor/turbine making the boiler modulate down; (4) scaled hot pipework, less common as a sudden change.

Discriminating checks you can do: time how long a litre jug takes to fill from hot vs cold at the nearest tap — that quantifies the restriction. Check the boiler inlet isolation valve is fully open. Watch the boiler display while hot runs: if it fires and holds temperature but flow is poor, the restriction is hydraulic (filter/exchanger); if it cycles or reports low flow, suspect the sensor.

Decision point: checking valves and timing flow is yours. Opening the boiler case, cleaning the plate exchanger, or touching anything on the gas side is a Gas Safe / registered heating engineer's job by law — book one and hand over your flow measurements; they'll shorten the visit.
The shower has started alternating hot and cold while I'm in it, but the boiler shows no fault code and other taps seem steady. What usually causes that?

Temperature swinging at one shower with a healthy boiler points at the shower itself or a pressure tug-of-war. Causes in order: (1) a failing thermostatic cartridge in the shower mixer — its wax element or seals wear and it hunts instead of holding temperature; (2) someone else's draw-off (a toilet refilling, a tap opening) dropping cold or hot pressure mid-shower — but you say other taps seem steady, and if the swings happen when you're alone in the house, that demotes this; (3) limescale in the shower head restricting flow so the mixer can't stabilise.

Discriminating checks: run the shower with nobody else using water — swings persisting solo convict the shower. Swap the head for a known-good one or run without it briefly: steady temperature bare means the head was the restriction. Also feel both feed pipes at the mixer; if both arrive steadily hot and cold while the output swings, the cartridge is mixing badly.

Decision point: heads and cartridges are DIY with the shower's isolators closed — a cartridge swap is a standard part and hand tools. Call a plumber if the feeds themselves fluctuate (that moves the fault back to the boiler or pressure balance) or if the mixer is a concealed in-wall unit with no access panel.
There's a damp, musty patch spreading on the ceiling directly below our bathroom, but I can't see any leak from the bath, shower, or pipes above. How do I find the source before it gets worse?

A ceiling stain with no visible leak above usually means a small, intermittent leak — it only weeps under specific conditions, which is why casual looking misses it. Suspects in order: (1) failed bath or shower sealant/tile grout — water escapes only while showering, running behind the tray and through the ceiling; statistically the commonest cause; (2) the bath waste or overflow connection, which leaks only when the bath is full or draining; (3) a pinhole in a supply pipe, which would usually grow steadily rather than intermittently; (4) condensation, unlikely to make a spreading defined patch.

Discriminating checks: map the stain with pencil marks and date them to see if it grows after showers, baths, or constantly. Then isolate by use: two days of baths only — growth stops? The shower screen/seal is convicted. Fill the bath, stand in it, and let it drain while someone watches below with the ceiling's access or a torch at the stain — the waste shows itself under load and body weight flexing the tray. A moisture meter or the back of a dry hand confirms active wetness vs an old stain.

Decision point: resealing and waste fittings are DIY. Stop and call a plumber if the stain grows with no fixture use at all (that's a pressurised pipe leaking continuously), if the ceiling bows or sags — saturated plasterboard can come down — or if the joists feel soft; that adds a builder to the job.

My toilet flushes weakly — the bowl swirls but solids often need a second flush. The cistern fills to the line and empties fast when I lift the flapper by hand in a bucket test... actually I haven't tested anything yet. Where should I start?

Start with the two things that decide flush power: how much water leaves the cistern, and how it enters the bowl. Causes in order: (1) rim jets or the siphon jet at the front of the bowl clogged with scale — the water arrives but with no push, extremely common in hard-water areas and fits a weak swirl; (2) the water level set too low or the flush valve opening only partially; (3) a partially blocked trapway — but that usually shows as the bowl water rising high then draining slowly, a different signature from a lazy swirl.

Discriminating checks: mark the cistern waterline — it should sit at or near the marked fill line; low level means adjust the fill valve first. Then pour a bucket of water quickly into the bowl: a strong flush from the bucket proves the trapway and drain are clear, so the fault is delivery (jets/valve). Poke the rim jets with a small mirror to look and a piece of wire or an old toothbrush to clear scale crust.

Decision point: jet cleaning, level adjustment, and flapper/valve swaps are all DIY with the isolator closed. Call a plumber if the bucket test also flushes poorly — that puts a partial obstruction in the trapway or drain, which is auger work.
There's a sewage smell in our bathroom that comes and goes, worst on windy days and after the bath empties. All the drains run freely. What could it be?

Free-running drains plus intermittent smell points to trap water being lost or sewer air being pushed in, not a blockage. Causes in order: (1) a trap siphoning dry — when the bath empties it can pull the water seal out of a nearby basin or shower trap, especially if the venting is poor; the timing after the bath empties fits this exactly; (2) a rarely used drain (guest shower, floor drain, washing machine standpipe) whose trap has simply evaporated; (3) a cracked or displaced vent/drain joint inside a wall letting air in on windy days when stack pressures swing.

Discriminating checks: after the bath empties, look and sniff at each trap in turn and run a cup of water into each — if the smell fades after refilling one, that trap was dry. Pour water into any unused drains too. Note whether the bath's own trap gurgles as it drains; gurgling is the sound of siphonage happening.

Decision point: refilling traps and fitting an anti-siphon (air admittance) trap is DIY. Call a plumber if every trap holds water yet the smell persists — that means an open joint or failed vent inside the structure, which needs smoke testing or opening up, and sewer gas in quantity is not something to live with while guessing.
A pipe under our kitchen floor has started ticking and creaking loudly whenever the hot water runs, and it stops a few minutes after. Is something about to burst?

Almost certainly not a burst warning — ticking that tracks hot water use and fades as things cool is thermal expansion: the hot pipe grows slightly in length and sticks-then-slips against joists, clips, or the holes it passes through, and each slip is a tick. It often starts when a pipe run is new, re-clipped tightly, or a boiler's flow temperature was raised.

Discriminating checks: the sound should begin within a minute of hot water running and be rhythmic with heating, not random. If you can see any of the run (under the sink, in a cupboard), watch for the pipe moving a fraction at a clip as it ticks. A burst or leak sounds entirely different — hissing, dripping, or a damp patch appearing.

Fix path: where the pipe passes through timber, ease the hole or wrap that section in felt/foam insulation so it can slide silently; loosen over-tight clips a fraction. All DIY, no water work beyond access. Decision point: call a plumber only if the noise comes with any sign of water — staining, a dropping boiler pressure on a sealed system, or a meter that creeps with taps off — because then the tick is a red herring next to a real leak.
Our outdoor tap has almost no flow since winter, though it worked fine last autumn. The inside taps are all normal. What's the likely story?

A single outdoor tap dying over winter, with the house unaffected, has a short suspect list: (1) frost damage — a split in the tap's feed pipe or the tap body itself from frozen water expanding; a split often hides inside the wall cavity and only shows when the tap is opened; (2) the tap's internal check valve or washer jammed with debris or perished over winter; (3) the isolation valve inside was closed for winter and only partly reopened — worth ruling out first because it's free.

Discriminating checks: fully open the internal isolator and retest. Then open the tap with a bucket under it and have someone watch the wall inside and out: water appearing inside the wall or running down the cavity when the tap runs means a frost split — close the isolator immediately. If everything stays dry but flow is a dribble, shut the isolator, unscrew the tap head, and inspect the washer and jumper — a swollen washer throttles flow exactly like this.

Decision point: washer and whole-tap replacement are easy DIY with the feed isolated. A split pipe inside the wall is a plumber job if it needs opening up and soldering in a new section — and leave the isolator closed until it's fixed.
The cold tap in the bathroom has started tasting and looking slightly cloudy with tiny white particles in the glass. The kitchen cold tap is clear. Should I be worried about the water supply?

One tap affected while the mains-fed kitchen tap is clear is reassuring and diagnostic: the bathroom cold is probably fed from a storage cistern in the loft (common in older houses), not directly from the mains. Causes in order: (1) limescale particles shedding from the cistern or the tap's own aerator and pipework — white grit that settles is classic scale; (2) debris or deterioration inside the storage cistern itself; (3) air in the line making water look milky — but air-cloudiness clears from the bottom of the glass upward within a minute and leaves no particles.

Discriminating checks: let a glass stand — particles that sink are scale/sediment; cloudiness that clears upward is just air. Remove and rinse the tap aerator and run the tap bare into a white bowl to see what comes out. Then, if you can do it safely, look into the loft cistern: it should have a fitted lid and clean water; debris, a missing lid, or worse in there ends the DIY phase.

Decision point: aerator cleaning is yours, and drinking water should come from the mains-fed kitchen tap meanwhile. A contaminated or uncovered storage cistern, or any doubt about what's in it, is a plumber's job to clean, disinfect, and re-cover — don't drink from that tap until it's sorted.
Our sealed heating system loses pressure slowly — I top it up from 1.5 bar to find it at 0.8 a week later. No visible leaks at any radiator. Where's the water going?

On a sealed system, falling pressure means water is leaving somewhere or the expansion vessel can no longer absorb it — and the two behave differently, so separate them first. Causes in order: (1) a failed or flat expansion vessel: pressure swings widely — high when hot (often lifting the safety valve at 3 bar, which then dribbles water away outside), low when cold; this fits 'no visible leak indoors' because the loss is through the pressure relief pipe outside; (2) a hidden leak under floors or in walls; (3) a weeping automatic air vent or radiator valve that evaporates as fast as it leaks, leaving only a faint stain or crust.

Discriminating checks: watch the gauge through one heating cycle — a swing of more than about 1 bar between cold and hot convicts the vessel. Check the relief pipe outlet outside for drips or a wet wall after the system has run hot. Run tissue around every valve and vent; look for green/white crust. If pressure falls steadily even with the system cold and unused for days, that's a true leak, not the vessel.

Decision point: tissue checks and gauge watching are yours. Vessel recharging/replacement and relief valves are heating-engineer work (the vessel sits on the sealed system and often inside the boiler case), and an underfloor leak hunt is a plumber with leak-detection kit — don't keep topping up indefinitely, because fresh water accelerates corrosion inside the system.
I can smell gas near our boiler cupboard. It's faint but definitely there when I open the door. What do I do?

Stop diagnosing and treat this as an emergency now. Do not investigate the source, do not open the boiler case, and do not operate anything electrical in that cupboard — no light switches, no unplugging — because a spark is exactly what you must avoid.

Do these things in order: (1) turn the gas off at the meter — the lever beside the meter, a quarter turn so it sits across the pipe; (2) open doors and windows to ventilate as you leave; (3) get everyone, including pets, out of the house; (4) from outside or a neighbour's house, call the gas emergency line (in the UK, 0800 111 999; in the US, your gas utility's emergency line or 911). They attend free, make the supply safe, and will tell you what they found.

Do not re-enter until they clear it, and don't light anything — no cigarettes, no candles — near the house meanwhile. A faint smell that concentrates in a closed cupboard is precisely the pattern that matters: gas has been accumulating where it can't disperse.

After the emergency team has made it safe, any repair is a registered gas engineer's job only — this is never DIY at any stage, and no part of the fix should be attempted before that emergency call.
The radiator in the spare room bleeds a lot of air every few weeks — I let out a long hiss before water appears. Other radiators need bleeding maybe once a year. Why this one?

One radiator repeatedly filling with gas while the rest behave means gas is being generated or drawn in at a rate the system can't vent elsewhere, and that radiator — often the highest or last on the run — is where it collects. Causes in order: (1) corrosion inside the system producing hydrogen gas: inhibitor-depleted water lets steel radiators corrode, and hydrogen is literally manufactured in the system; it collects at the top of the most convenient radiator; (2) air being drawn in through a micro-leak or a pump-side joint on a vented system each time the pump runs; (3) the automatic air vent elsewhere being stuck shut, so this radiator becomes the system's only vent.

Discriminating check, and it's a good one (carefully, adults only): hold a lit match to the bleed screw as you vent a small amount of gas. Hydrogen from corrosion pops with a small flame; plain air just blows the match out. Also check the water that follows — black, gritty water supports the corrosion story; clean water supports drawn-in air.

Decision point: bleeding is DIY; the cure differs by cause. Hydrogen/corrosion means the system needs flushing and fresh inhibitor — a heating engineer or confident DIY with drain-down, but on a sealed system leave it to an engineer. If it's drawn-in air on a vented system, finding the suction leak is engineer work too.
My kitchen sink makes a glugging sound and the water in the trap bubbles when the dishwasher drains into the same waste. Everything still drains away. Is a blockage forming?

Probably not a blockage yet — glugging with free drainage is an air problem, not a water problem. When the dishwasher pumps out, it pushes a slug of water and air down the shared waste; the air displaces through your sink trap because the waste run can't vent fast enough, and you hear it as glugs and see it as bubbles. Causes in order: (1) no proper venting on that waste run, or an air admittance valve that's stuck or was never fitted; (2) a partial restriction far down the run slowing air escape — possible, but then you'd expect drainage to be slowing too; (3) the dishwasher hose connected above the trap without a high loop, letting drain air and odours push back.

Discriminating checks: fill the sink and pull the plug — if the sink itself drains silently and fast, the run is clear and it's venting. Watch whether the trap's water level gets pulled low after the dishwasher cycle (dip a fingertip or check for smells afterwards): a trap left low is the real risk, since sewer air then has a path in.

Decision point: fitting an anti-siphon trap or an air admittance valve under the sink is straightforward DIY. Call a plumber if the trap is regularly emptied (smell follows), if drainage starts slowing, or if the run is shared with a toilet — that changes the venting design entirely.

Our gas furnace starts up, runs for about three minutes, shuts off, then does it again ten minutes later — all evening. The house never quite reaches the set temperature. What's the pattern telling me?

That run-stop-run pattern is short-cycling, and the three-minute runtime is the key measurement: the furnace is being shut down by something shortly after firing, long before the thermostat is satisfied (the thermostat would keep it running, since the house stays cold). Causes in order: (1) overheating trip — the high-limit switch kills the burner because heat isn't leaving the furnace: a clogged filter is the number-one cause, followed by blocked vents or a failing blower; (2) a dirty flame sensor, though that usually cuts the burner within seconds, not minutes; (3) an oversized furnace or a thermostat fault — lower on the list given the consistent short runtime.

Discriminating check, free and first: pull the filter and look at it against a light. If it's grey and matted, fit a new one and watch a full cycle — problem gone, done. Also walk the house and open every supply vent and return grille; closed returns starve airflow the same way.

Decision point: filters and vents are yours. If it still short-cycles on a clean filter, stop there: limit switches, flame sensors, and blower motors live inside the cabinet alongside gas and mains wiring — that's an HVAC technician's job, and repeated limit trips are the furnace protecting itself, not a nuisance to override.
The air conditioning runs constantly on hot days but the air from the vents feels barely cool, and the house slowly loses ground. It worked fine last summer. Where do I start?

Barely-cool air with a constantly running system means it's producing some cooling but far too little. Measure first: hold a thermometer at a return grille, then at the nearest supply vent. A healthy system drops the air about 8-11°C (15-20°F) across that path. A small drop narrows the fault. Causes in order: (1) a filthy filter or a frosted evaporator coil strangling airflow — check the filter, and peek at the indoor coil or suction line for ice; an iced coil also explains 'worked last year, faded this year' as airflow declined; (2) a dirty outdoor condenser coil or a failed condenser fan, so heat can't be rejected outside; (3) low refrigerant from a slow leak — possible, but it's third, not first, and it's the one you can't touch.

Discriminating checks: new filter; outdoor unit — is the fan spinning and the air coming off it hot? Is the thick suction line at the outdoor unit cold and sweating (good) or room temperature (bad)? Any ice anywhere means switch to fan-only for a few hours to thaw before judging further.

Decision point: filters, coil rinsing outside with a gentle hose, and clearing vegetation are DIY. Anything involving refrigerant — gauges, topping up, leak repair — is licensed work by law and by safety; never buy a 'top-up' without a leak diagnosis.
One radiator is hot at the bottom but stone cold across the top half, while the others are hot all over. The system was fine last year. Likely fix?

Cold at the top with a hot bottom is the textbook signature of air trapped in that radiator: air rises, occupies the top, and hot water simply can't fill the space it sits in. The fact that it's one radiator and the rest are fine rules out boiler or pump problems — those would show everywhere.

The check and the fix are the same act: with the heating on or recently on, open the bleed screw at the top corner of that radiator with a radiator key, a cloth underneath, and close it the moment water — not air — appears. If you get a satisfying hiss first, the diagnosis is confirmed as it cures itself. Afterwards, on a sealed system, check the boiler pressure gauge: bleeding drops pressure slightly, and if it has fallen below about 1 bar cold, top up via the filling loop to 1-1.5 bar.

Decision point: entirely DIY. Escalate only in two cases: the radiator refills with air within days (that points to corrosion gas or air being drawn in — a system problem), or bleeding produces no air and no water at all, which suggests a blocked bleed or a sludge-filled radiator — sludge (cold bottom, hot top is the inverse pattern) is a power-flush conversation with a heating engineer.
Our living room is always two or three degrees colder than the thermostat shows, and the thermostat is in the hallway. The hallway feels fine. Is the thermostat faulty?

Probably not faulty — misplaced for the room you care about. The thermostat controls the whole system from wherever it sits, and a hallway thermostat lives in different conditions: hallways gain heat from every room's leakage, often sit near the front door's draught patterns or away from them, and have no one sitting still in them for hours. If the hallway genuinely is at the set temperature while the living room lags, the thermostat is doing its job accurately in the wrong place. Other contributors in order: (1) living-room radiators undersized, unbalanced (starved of flow), or blocked by furniture/sofas; (2) heat loss concentrated in the living room — a chimney flue, single-glazed bay, or external walls on two sides; (3) an actual thermostat calibration error — testable, and last.

Discriminating checks: put an ordinary thermometer beside the thermostat for an evening — if it agrees with the display, the stat is honest. Then compare radiator surface temperatures: a lukewarm living-room radiator while others are hot means balancing (open its lockshield valve more, throttle the hottest radiators slightly). Hot radiator but cold room means heat loss, not heating.

Decision point: thermometers, balancing, and moving furniture are DIY. Relocating a wired thermostat means mains-voltage wiring for many models — an electrician or heating engineer does that; a wireless stat with the receiver swapped by an engineer and the sensor placed in the living room is usually the clean cure.
Since we had a smart thermostat fitted, the boiler fires up for a minute or two at a time, dozens of times a day, and our gas use has gone up. The old dial thermostat didn't do this. What changed?

The new stat is almost certainly controlling differently, not the boiler failing. Smart stats typically use tight temperature bands or TPI (time-proportional) control: instead of the old stat's wide swing — fire until well past target, coast down — they pulse the boiler in short bursts to hold temperature precisely. Dozens of one-to-two-minute fires fits that exactly. The problem: very short burns are inefficient for many boilers (each start wastes a purge and warm-up), and some boilers are harmed by rapid cycling, so gas use can rise despite the 'smarter' control.

Discriminating checks: read the stat's settings for cycle rate / minimum on-time / control mode — many have an 'oil/gas boiler' profile or a hysteresis (swing) setting. Set a wider swing (e.g. 0.5-1°C) or the manufacturer's boiler-optimised mode and compare a week's firing counts in the app history. Also confirm the stat was wired/configured for a boiler, not left on an electric-heating profile with a very high cycle rate.

Decision point: settings are yours and reversible. If the stat offers no suitable boiler mode, that's a product mismatch — a heating engineer can advise or fit a stat with proper boiler control (e.g. OpenTherm modulation if your boiler supports it, which ends short-cycling by turning the flame down instead of off).
The upstairs radiators are hot but the two downstairs ones are barely warm, on a system with the boiler in the kitchen. It got worse after I bled the upstairs radiators. What links those facts?

Your bleeding is the link: on a sealed system, letting air out also lets pressure out, and if the pressure has dropped, the pump can no longer push water round the full circuit — the radiators that lose out are the ones hardest to reach, and upstairs winning over downstairs tells you flow is marginal overall. Causes in order: (1) system pressure too low after bleeding — check the gauge before anything else: below ~1 bar cold, circulation suffers; (2) an unbalanced system where the upstairs radiators, freshly bled and free-flowing, now hog the flow (water takes the easiest path); (3) a weakening pump or sludge narrowing downstairs pipework — real, but check the free causes first.

Discriminating checks: read the pressure gauge cold. If low, top up via the filling loop to 1-1.5 bar and retest — instant improvement convicts pressure. If pressure is fine, feel the downstairs radiator flow and return pipes: flow hot, radiator cool means the water is short-circuiting elsewhere (balancing); both pipes cool means no flow arriving (pump/sludge/valve).

Decision point: topping up and balancing via lockshield valves are standard DIY. A failed pump, a system that keeps losing pressure after top-up (a leak or expansion vessel fault), or sludge needing a power flush belongs to a heating engineer.
Our AC blows cold air fine, but there's a musty, old-socks smell from the vents for the first few minutes each time it starts. It fades once it's running. What makes that smell?

A smell that appears at start-up and fades is usually microbial growth sitting in the wettest part of the system — the evaporator coil and its condensate drain pan — whose odour gets blown out in the first minutes before diluting. Causes in order: (1) a slimy biofilm on the coil or in a stagnant drain pan (the classic 'dirty sock' syndrome); (2) a condensate drain that's partially blocked, leaving standing water in the pan between cycles — check whether the drain line drips freely outside while the unit runs; (3) a saturated, old filter holding odour — cheap to rule out.

Discriminating checks: replace the filter and note any change. Look at the condensate drain outlet while the AC runs: a steady drip means drainage works; nothing, plus smell, means water is sitting somewhere. Shine a torch at the coil through an access panel if there is one — visible slime or a pan full of water confirms it.

Decision point: filter changes and flushing the drain line with a wet-vac from outside are DIY. Coil deep-cleaning with the cabinet opened, or any UV/biocide treatment inside the air handler, is a technician job — the coil fins are delicate and the cabinet contains mains wiring.
One bedroom is always stuffy and warm in summer even though its vent blows, and the vent in the hallway blasts like a hairdryer. The system cools the rest of the house evenly. What's the imbalance?

Even cooling elsewhere plus one weak room plus one over-strong vent is an airflow distribution problem, not a cooling-capacity problem — the cold exists, it's just going to the wrong places. Causes in order: (1) damper settings: the hallway branch damper wide open and the bedroom's partly closed (or a flex duct to the bedroom kinked, crushed by stored boxes in the attic, or disconnected at a joint — very common); (2) the bedroom's return path blocked: supply air can't enter a closed room if air can't leave — a tight door with no undercut or return grille pressurises the room and chokes its own supply; (3) a long, undersized bedroom run losing pressure.

Discriminating checks: tissue test at the bedroom vent with the door open vs closed — if flow collapses when the door closes, it's the return path, and a door undercut or transfer grille is the cure. In the attic, follow the bedroom duct with your hands: a crushed or detached section announces itself. Compare vent flow before and after partly closing the hallway damper — if the bedroom picks up, it was balance all along.

Decision point: dampers, door undercuts, and re-taping a duct joint are DIY. Redesigning duct sizes or adding a return is an HVAC contractor job — but bring them your tissue-test and attic findings and the visit gets short.
Our boiler makes a loud kettling noise — like a kettle coming to the boil, with rumbles — for a few minutes after it fires, then settles. Heating works fine otherwise. Should I be worried?

Kettling is localised boiling inside the heat exchanger: water in one spot gets hot enough to form steam bubbles that collapse noisily as they move into cooler water. Heating still 'working' while it kettles fits — the boiler delivers heat, just inefficiently and under stress. Causes in order: (1) limescale or sludge coating the inside of the heat exchanger, insulating the metal so the water film against it boils — the classic cause in hard-water areas; (2) flow through the boiler too slow (pump speed low, a nearly closed valve, sludge elsewhere) so water lingers and overheats; (3) a failing pump on its way out.

Discriminating checks: does turning the pump speed up (if it has a speed switch) quiet it? Faster flow suppressing the noise supports the flow/scale pair over a mechanical fault. Check how quickly the noise starts after firing — within a minute suggests heavy scale right at the exchanger.

Decision point: this one is mostly hands-off for DIY: the cure is a chemical cleanse or power flush of the system, or exchanger descaling inside the boiler — heating-engineer work, and inside the boiler case it's registered-engineer territory if gas. Don't ignore it long-term: kettling wastes fuel and the scale that causes it eventually cracks exchangers.
The heating comes on at night even though I've set the thermostat schedule to be off until 6am. The display shows a little snowflake icon sometimes. Is the thermostat broken?

Almost certainly not broken — the snowflake is the clue: that's frost protection. Most thermostats and boiler controls have a built-in safeguard that fires the heating if the sensed temperature falls toward 5°C or so, regardless of your schedule, to stop pipes freezing. On cold nights the house drifts down to that threshold, the boiler runs a short cycle, and the temperature recovers — exactly the behaviour you're describing.

Discriminating checks: note the room temperature shown when you catch it running — if it's around 5-7°C, frost protection is confirmed. Check the manual or settings menu for 'frost protection' or 'freeze protection' — on many stats the threshold is adjustable within a small range, and on some the boiler itself has a separate frost stat that also responds to an outdoor sensor.

Decision point: leave it on — it's protecting the house, and the short cycles cost little. Only involve a heating engineer if the boiler fires at mild temperatures (say above 10°C), which would suggest a faulty sensor reading cold — and even then, compare the stat's reading against a standalone thermometer first to prove the sensor is lying before paying for a visit.
There's a pool of water under our indoor AC unit and the carpet nearby is damp. The AC still cools. Where's the water from and how urgent is it?

An air conditioner makes litres of condensate a day, and a pool under the indoor unit means that water is escaping instead of draining. It still cooling tells you the refrigeration side is fine. Causes in order: (1) a blocked condensate drain line — algae and slime choke the trap or line until the pan overflows; the commonest cause by far; (2) a cracked or rusted drain pan; (3) the coil icing up and meltwater overwhelming or missing the pan — check for ice on the coil or the thick refrigerant line.

Discriminating checks: find the drain's outside outlet while the unit runs — nothing dripping there while the unit cools hard means the line is blocked. A wet-vac on that outside outlet for a minute often pulls the plug of slime out and you hear the pan drain. If the line runs free and water still pools, the pan itself or an overflowing secondary pan is at fault.

Urgency and decision point: treat it as soon — not an emergency today, but condensate rots flooring and grows mould fast. Clearing the drain line from outside with a wet-vac is safe DIY (no cabinet opening). A cracked pan or anything requiring the air handler opened goes to a technician, and if you see ice, switch the system to fan-only to thaw before anyone works on it.

Our furnace blower runs constantly even when there's no heating or cooling call, and setting the thermostat fan to AUTO doesn't stop it. It started after a very cold snap. What could be holding it on?

A blower that won't stop after a cold snap has two families of causes, and the cold snap is a strong hint toward one of them: (1) the high-limit switch tripped hard during the cold weather (when the furnace ran longest) and on many furnaces a limit fault locks the blower ON deliberately — it's a safety behaviour, blowing air to cool a furnace it believes overheated; (2) a stuck blower relay or a thermostat wire short (the G wire calling for fan continuously), or the thermostat itself failed with its fan contact closed.

Discriminating checks: remove the thermostat from its wall plate (most pop off). If the blower stops, the stat or its wiring is commanding the fan — a stat swap is DIY at low voltage. If it keeps running with the stat off the wall, the command is inside the furnace: check for a blower door switch not fully depressed by a poorly seated panel, then stop.

Decision point: thermostat and panel checks are yours. A furnace holding its blower on because of a limit event is telling you it tripped for a reason — clogged filter, blocked vents, failing blower — and diagnosing limit circuits inside the cabinet, among gas and mains connections, is a technician's job. Don't just leave it running: find out what tripped it.
The radiators on our top floor are lukewarm while the ground floor ones are hot, on an old open-vented system with a tank in the loft. It was the reverse problem last year. Where do I look?

On an open-vented system, top-floor radiators starving usually means the water isn't being pushed up there with enough vigour, or the feed from the loft tank can't replace what's circulating. Causes in order: (1) low water level in the feed-and-expansion tank in the loft — a stuck ballcock or a frozen/scaled feed means the system's head of pressure drops and the highest radiators lose out first; (2) air collected in the top radiators; (3) the pump weakening or set too slow; (4) sludge settled in the top-floor pipework — less likely to change year to year.

Discriminating checks: loft first — look in the small feed tank: the water should sit a few inches deep with the ballcock free. If it's nearly dry or the ballcock is seized up, you've found it. Bleed a top radiator: air out then nothing (no water following) also points to a starved feed rather than a full system.

Decision point: freeing a ballcock and bleeding are DIY (mind the loft access and the tank's overflow). If the tank is full and bleeding gives water yet the rads stay lukewarm, the pump or circulation is at fault — a heating engineer, since pump swaps on an old vented system involve drain-down and valves that may not have moved in decades.
Our heat pump ices up on the outdoor unit in winter until it's a solid white block, and then the house goes cold. Defrost cycles used to clear it. What's changed?

A heat pump frosting in cold, damp weather is normal; staying frosted is not. The defrost cycle should periodically reverse the system to melt the coil clear. If ice now wins, causes in order: (1) the defrost control or its coil temperature sensor failing, so defrost starts late, ends early, or never starts; (2) a failed outdoor fan or a coil so dirty that airflow is poor — poor airflow makes frosting dramatically worse and defrost less effective; (3) low refrigerant, which makes the coil run colder than design and frost faster than defrost can clear; (4) meltwater refreezing at the base because the unit's drainage is blocked or the unit sits in a puddle of its own melt.

Discriminating checks you can do: watch one full cycle — does the fan stop and the unit steam (defrost happening) at all? Steam but still iced means defrost runs too short (sensor/control). No defrost at all over hours of frosting means control failure. Clear leaves and debris from the coil and make sure meltwater can drain away from the base.

Decision point: cleaning the coil and drainage is DIY. Defrost boards, sensors, fans, and anything refrigerant-related are technician work. Don't chip ice off with tools — the coil and refrigerant lines damage easily, and a punctured line turns a control fault into a major repair.
A radiator valve in our bedroom drips slowly from the spindle where the head sits, leaving a greenish crust. The radiator heats fine. Is this a big job?

No — a weep at the valve spindle (the pin the thermostatic head pushes on) with greenish crust is a classic minor leak: the gland seal around the pin has worn, and the crust is copper salts from water that evaporates as fast as it escapes, which is why the drip seems trivially slow. It will not heal itself, and over a season it wastes inhibitor-treated water and stains the floor.

Check first: does it drip only when the valve is turned (pin moving), or constantly? A drip on movement only is early-stage gland wear. Try the easy fix: remove the thermostatic head (it unscrews by hand), and gently tighten the small gland nut around the pin a quarter turn — many valves allow this and it re-compresses the packing. Work the pin up and down a few times with the flat of a screwdriver to free any stickiness.

Decision point: gland tightening and head swaps are DIY with a cloth for drips. If the gland nut is already fully home and it still weeps, the valve body needs replacing, which means draining that radiator or freezing the pipes — a plumber's half-hour job, or confident DIY with a drain-down. On a sealed system, remember to restore pressure afterwards.
Since the weather turned cold, our windows stream with condensation every morning and the bathroom mirror never really clears. The heating works. Is this a heating problem at all?

Mostly not — it's a moisture-balance problem, and heating is only one of three levers. Overnight, warm moist air from breathing, showers, and drying clothes meets the coldest surfaces in the house — window glass — and condenses. Causes in order: (1) ventilation too low for the moisture produced: extractor fans unused, broken, or too weak, trickle vents closed, and a sealed-up modern house holding it all in; (2) moisture production high: clothes dried on radiators, unvented tumble dryer, long showers; (3) cold surfaces made colder by heating being off overnight, so the glass sits below dew point for hours.

Discriminating checks: a cheap hygrometer tells the truth — indoor relative humidity persistently above 60% in winter convicts ventilation/moisture, not the boiler. Check the bathroom extractor actually extracts: hold a tissue at the grille while it runs; it should grip firmly. Note whether condensation forms between the panes of a double-glazed unit — that's a failed sealed unit, a different fault entirely (glazier, not heating).

Decision point: run extractors during and 20 minutes after showers, open trickle vents, dry clothes in a vented room, keep a low background heat — all behaviour, all DIY. Call a glazier for between-pane fogging, and a builder only if you find damp in walls rather than on glass — surface condensation and penetrating damp are different diagnoses.
A breaker in our panel trips every few days, always in the evening. It feeds the kitchen sockets. Resetting it works fine and nothing seems faulty. What's the pattern pointing to?

Evening-only tripping on a kitchen circuit with no single faulty appliance is the signature of cumulative load: evenings are when the kettle, oven, microwave, dishwasher, and washing machine overlap, and the breaker is doing its job against a circuit asked for more than its rating — a breaker that trips instantly on reset suggests a short; one that trips after minutes of heavy use suggests thermal overload. Causes in order: (1) simple overload from simultaneous appliances; (2) one appliance drawing more than it should as it ages (a failing oven element leaking to earth can also trip an RCD/RCBO rather than the breaker — note which device actually trips, because that distinction splits the diagnosis); (3) a loose connection in the circuit warming under load.

Discriminating checks: note exactly which device trips — overcurrent breaker vs RCD/GFCI trip means different faults (overload/short vs earth leakage). Then run the evening routine minus one big appliance at a time; the combination that stops tripping names the load. Feel the breaker after a trip: warm is consistent with overload.

Decision point: load management and observation are yours. Anything inside the consumer unit/panel — tightening, swapping breakers, splitting circuits — is electrician-only: the busbar side stays live even with the main switch off. If an RCD is the one tripping with no load pattern, stop experimenting and book an electrician; earth leakage is a shock-risk fault, not an inconvenience.
Three outlets in our living room have all stopped working at once, but the breaker hasn't tripped and the rest of the house is fine. Any ideas before I call an electrician?

Three dead outlets on one circuit with the breaker on usually means the circuit is interrupted at a single point, and the most common single point is protection you may not know you have. Causes in order: (1) a tripped GFCI/RCD outlet upstream — often in the same room, a bathroom, the garage, or outside — whose trip kills every outlet wired through it ('load' side); the dead outlets are frequently the ones furthest from the panel, which fits a chain going down together; (2) a failed connection at the first dead outlet — outlets are often daisy-chained through each other's terminals, so one burnt or loose connection kills everything downstream of it; (3) a tripped breaker that looks on — some sit in a middle position and fool the eye.

Discriminating checks: hunt for any outlet with TEST/RESET buttons — kitchen, bathroom, garage, porch, even the opposite wall — press RESET and retest the dead three. Then flip the suspect breaker fully OFF and back ON to rule out the middle-position trick.

Decision point: resetting a GFCI and a breaker is user-level. If neither restores power, the fault is a failed connection inside an outlet box: that's an electrician for most people — the wiring inside can be live from unexpected directions, and burnt terminals need replacing, not wiggling.
The lights in our house dip noticeably every time the fridge motor or the AC kicks on. It's been happening for years and nothing has failed. Should I care?

A brief dip when a big motor starts is physics, not necessarily a fault: motors draw several times their running current for a fraction of a second, and that inrush sags the voltage on shared wiring. Whether to care depends on depth and trend. Causes in order: (1) normal inrush on a circuit with some impedance — long runs, older wiring; (2) a deteriorating connection somewhere (at the panel, meter, or a junction) adding resistance, so the same inrush causes a bigger sag than it used to; (3) a loose or corroding neutral — the dangerous one, because a failing neutral makes voltages swing both down AND up, and the up-swings kill electronics.

Discriminating checks: do some lights get BRIGHTER while others dim when a big load starts? Brightening anywhere is the neutral-fault signature — treat that as urgent. Is the dip house-wide or one circuit? House-wide points toward the service/panel; one circuit points to that run. Has it deepened over the years? A worsening trend matters more than the dip itself.

Decision point: observing and noting which pattern you have is yours, and it decides the urgency. Any of — brightening lights, flicker at random with no motor starting, buzzing or heat at the panel — means an electrician promptly, and the utility if the fault is on their side of the meter. Panel internals and service connections are never DIY.

I plugged a space heater into a bedroom outlet and after twenty minutes the plug was hot and there's a faint scorch mark around one slot of the outlet. The heater works fine elsewhere. What's wrong and what do I do?

Treat that outlet as out of service from now until it's replaced: a hot plug and scorch mark mean high resistance at the contact between plug and outlet — the outlet's contacts have lost their grip (worn, sprung, or heat-damaged), and the resistance turns the connection itself into a small heater. That is a genuine fire mechanism, and it gets worse each time it's used, because heat further weakens the contacts. The heater 'working fine elsewhere' confirms the appliance is innocent and the outlet is the fault.

What to do: stop using that outlet entirely — don't 'just use it for low-power things'; a phone charger draws little, but the damaged contact is unpredictable. Don't use the heater in that room until it's fixed. If there's any smell of burning now, or the outlet is warm with nothing plugged in, switch the circuit off at the breaker and treat it as urgent.

Decision point: outlet replacement is where the DIY line sits differently by jurisdiction and skill, but the safe advice stands: this is an electrician's short job — the box needs inspection for heat damage to the wire insulation behind it, which is the part you can't judge from the front. A plug that was heat-exposed should be replaced too, not reused. No further diagnosis by plugging things in — the symptom you have is already the diagnosis.
The bathroom GFCI outlet trips every time I use the hair dryer, but the dryer works fine in the bedroom and the GFCI resets and holds with other things. Who's lying, the dryer or the outlet?

Possibly neither — they may both be marginal and only fail in combination. A GFCI trips on earth leakage, not overload, and a hair dryer is a harsh test: high current, heat, vibration, and often slightly leaky heating elements as they age. Causes in order: (1) the dryer's element or cord leaking a few milliamps to earth — under the trip threshold of a healthy GFCI at low heat settings but over it on full blast, and a bedroom outlet without GFCI protection simply never reports the leak; (2) a GFCI that's grown hypersensitive with age — they do drift and nuisance-trip; (3) moisture in the bathroom outlet box adding its own leakage path.

Discriminating checks: try the dryer in a DIFFERENT GFCI outlet (kitchen). Trips there too — the dryer is leaking; retire it, because a leaking heating appliance in a bathroom is exactly what the protection exists for. Runs fine elsewhere — the bathroom GFCI is the suspect. Also test the bathroom GFCI with its own TEST button and with a small load like a phone charger.

Decision point: swapping the appliance between outlets is safe diagnosis. Replacing a GFCI outlet is an electrician job for most people — bathroom wiring and water-adjacent work carry rules beyond the swap itself. Don't solve it by using the dryer in the bathroom on an extension from another room: that defeats the protection in the one room that needs it most.
One ceiling light flickers irregularly — not in time with anything switching — while the other lights on the same circuit are steady. The bulb is new. What should I check?

One fitting flickering while its circuit-mates stay steady localises the fault to that fitting, its switch, or the bulb's contact — the supply to the circuit is proven good by the steady lights. Causes in order: (1) a poor contact in the bulb holder: a bent centre contact, slight corrosion, or the bulb not fully seated — irregular flicker that changes if you tap the fitting is the giveaway; (2) a loose wire connection in the fitting's terminal block or the ceiling rose, arcing microscopically as it warms and cools; (3) an incompatible dimmer — if this light is on a dimmer and the new bulb is an LED, mismatched dimmers flicker exactly like this, often worse at low settings; (4) the switch contacts wearing.

Discriminating checks, power off at the breaker first for anything beyond bulb swaps: reseat the bulb firmly; try the bulb in another fitting and a known bulb here — the flicker follows the bulb or stays with the fitting, splitting the suspects in half. If there's a dimmer, test at full brightness.

Decision point: bulb swaps with power on are normal use; anything involving the fitting's wiring is breaker-off work, and if you're not confident identifying the circuit and testing it's dead, it's an electrician. A loose connection that arcs is a fire risk in slow motion — don't leave a flickering fitting flickering for months while deciding.
Half the outlets in our new extension work, half don't, and the dead ones are all on one wall. The extension passed inspection a year ago. What single fault explains that pattern?

Dead outlets grouped on one wall, on a circuit that's partly alive, with a clean inspection a year ago, points to a single connection failure at the boundary between the live group and the dead group — most likely the last working outlet or the first dead one, because outlets on a radial/ring are wired through each other. Causes in order: (1) a conductor worked loose or burnt at a terminal in the junction between the groups — a screw terminal that was slightly under-tightened cooks slowly under load cycles until it lets go; (2) a damaged cable in that wall — a picture hook or screw driven into a cable run can sever or nearly sever a conductor (think about anything hung on that wall recently); (3) a failed back-to-back connection where the wall's outlets feed through.

Discriminating checks: identify the exact boundary — the working outlet nearest the dead ones is suspect number one. Any recent screws or nails in that wall above or beside the dead outlets? That's suspect two. Flickering or crackling from the boundary outlet before it died would confirm the loose-terminal story.

Decision point: mapping the boundary and remembering the picture hooks is yours, and it will halve the electrician's bill. Opening outlets and repairing conductors is electrician work — a heat-damaged terminal usually means damaged wire insulation inside the box that needs cutting back to clean copper, judged in person. Keep load off that circuit's damaged section meanwhile.
There's a buzzing sound coming from our breaker panel, and one breaker feels warmer than the others. Everything still works. How do I handle this?

Carefully, and mostly by calling an electrician today rather than diagnosing it yourself — a buzzing panel with a warm breaker is one of the symptoms where the correct move is to limit your interaction with it. What it usually means: a breaker whose internal contacts are deteriorating or a loose connection on the busbar, arcing or vibrating under load; the warmth is resistive heating at a failing joint. These faults progress: the heat damages neighbouring breakers and insulation, and panels are where electrical fires start.

What you may safely do: note which breaker is warm and what it feeds; reduce load on that circuit (unplug or stop using the big loads on it); look — without touching anything inside — for discolouration, a burning smell, or scorch marks around that breaker; take a photo for the electrician. Do NOT remove the panel cover, do NOT tighten or wiggle the breaker, and don't keep resetting anything. If you smell burning, hear crackling/sizzling rather than a hum, or see any scorching, switch off the main breaker if you can do so without opening anything, and call an emergency electrician (and your utility if the meter area is involved).

The electrician will likely replace the breaker and inspect the busbar for heat damage — a modest job if caught now, a panel replacement if the busbar has cooked. This is precisely the 'call a professional and why' case: the fault is at the one point in the house where every circuit's energy converges and the supply side cannot be isolated by you at all.
Our electric shower keeps cutting out mid-use and the pull-cord switch feels stiff and sometimes crackles. It comes back on after a few minutes. What's failing?

An electric shower is one of the heaviest loads in a house, and cut-out plus a crackling, stiff pull switch points at the switch itself: its contacts carry the full shower current, and as they wear and pit, resistance rises, the switch heats, and either its own thermal effects or the shower's internal overheat cut-out (tripping from poor supply behaviour) ends the cycle — then it cools and works again, which is why 'comes back after a few minutes' fits a heat-driven fault. Causes in order: (1) failing pull-cord isolator switch contacts — the crackle is arcing, and arcing is the sound of a switch dying; (2) the shower's thermal cut-out tripping because scaled heating elements overheat the water locally; (3) a loose terminal in the shower unit or switch cooking under load.

Stop using it. A crackling switch handling 40+ amps is a fire risk in a bathroom, the worst combination in the house. There is no safe user-level check that adds information — the symptom set is already conclusive enough to act.

Decision point: electrician, promptly, and keep the circuit off at the breaker until they've been. The switch (and possibly the shower) will be replaced and the cable inspected for heat damage. Bathroom circuits, water, and the highest continuous load in the home — this is licensed work on every count, and not a 'see how it goes' fault.
I reset a tripped breaker and it trips again instantly with a pop, every time, even though I've unplugged everything on that circuit. What's different about this from an overload?

Instant tripping on reset, with loads unplugged, is a fundamentally different fault from overload: an overload breaker trips after seconds-to-minutes of excess current and feels warm; an instant, repeatable trip with a pop means a hard short circuit or a dead short to earth somewhere on the fixed wiring or a still-connected load — a large fault current flows the moment you energise it. Suspects in order: (1) something still connected that you've forgotten — a wired-in appliance, a water heater, an outdoor socket, a fridge on that circuit; (2) a damaged cable — rodent damage in a loft, a screw through a cable, a crushed run; (3) water inside an outdoor fitting or junction box shorting live to earth; (4) a failed fixed appliance — boiler, immersion heater, oven element.

What you may do: leave the breaker OFF — repeatedly forcing a short is how cables get damaged further. Unplug and also switch off every fused spur and fixed appliance on that circuit, then try ONE reset. If it holds, reconnect things one at a time until the culprit trips it. If it trips with absolutely everything isolated, the fault is in the fixed wiring.

Decision point: the isolation game is safe and often finds a failed appliance. Fixed-wiring shorts are electrician work with test instruments (insulation resistance testing) — that's how the damaged section gets located without guesswork.
The LED bulbs in our kitchen buzz and shimmer slightly on the dimmer, but they're fine in a normal lamp. The dimmer is ten years old and the bulbs are new 'dimmable' LEDs. Is something dying?

Nothing is dying — you have a compatibility mismatch, the commonest LED complaint there is. Your old dimmer was built for incandescent bulbs: it chops the mains waveform (leading-edge) and expects a heavy resistive load. LEDs draw tiny current through electronic drivers, and a 'dimmable' LED on the wrong dimmer gets an unstable chopped supply — the driver hunts, producing buzz (often from the bulb or the dimmer itself) and visible shimmer, worst at low settings. Causes in order: (1) leading-edge dimmer vs LED drivers that want trailing-edge; (2) load too low — the total wattage of your LEDs may sit below the dimmer's minimum load, so it can't regulate at all; (3) mixed bulb brands on one dimmer behaving differently.

Discriminating checks: put one incandescent or halogen bulb (if you still have one) in the circuit — if everything calms down, the dimmer needed the load and the diagnosis is confirmed. Test the LEDs at full brightness: stable at full but shimmering low is classic dimmer mismatch, not faulty bulbs (you've already shown they're fine in a lamp).

Decision point: the fix is a modern LED-rated (trailing-edge) dimmer with a suitable minimum load, or smart bulbs on a plain switch. Swapping a dimmer module is mains wiring — breaker off, prove dead, and if that sentence isn't routine for you, it's an electrician's twenty minutes.
Our doorbell transformer area in the consumer unit hums loudly and the bell has started ringing faintly by itself at night. Coincidence?

Probably not coincidence — the two symptoms share the transformer and the bell circuit. A doorbell transformer hums when its laminations loosen with age and heat; a louder hum means it's working harder or failing. The phantom faint ringing suggests the bell is receiving partial voltage when it shouldn't: causes in order: (1) the transformer failing and its output misbehaving; (2) the bell-push switch sticking or its contacts damp and partially conducting — outdoor pushes live in the weather, and a damp, corroded push can pass a trickle that makes an electronic chime murmur or a traditional bell tremble; (3) chafed bell wire shorting intermittently against something in a wall or door frame.

Discriminating checks: disconnect the wire at the bell push (power to the transformer off first at the breaker, since you'll be near the consumer unit — actually the push is low-voltage, but be tidy) — if the phantom ringing stops with the push out of circuit, the push is the culprit; replace it for a few pounds/dollars. Feel the transformer: too hot to hold comfortably means it's failing regardless.

Decision point: the bell push and the bell itself are low-voltage DIY. The transformer is wired into the consumer unit — mains work in the one box you shouldn't open; a hot or loudly humming transformer gets an electrician to swap it, and they'll likely solve the hum and the ghost rings in the same visit.
Since a thunderstorm last week, two appliances in different rooms have died and one circuit's RCD trips randomly a few times a day. Is one event behind all of this?

Quite possibly yes — a nearby lightning strike or the resulting surge can wound a house's electrics in exactly this scattered way, and 'wounded, not killed' components fail over the following days. The story hangs together: a surge stresses appliance power supplies (the two deaths), and it can also damage insulation marginally in wiring or appliances so that earth leakage appears intermittently — the random RCD trips — especially when the damaged item warms up, gets damp, or vibrates. Causes in order: (1) surge-damaged appliance(s) now leaking to earth intermittently — the same class of event that killed two outright; (2) a surge-damaged RCD itself, now tripping below its rated threshold; (3) damaged cable insulation in the fixed wiring — less common but the one that matters most.

Discriminating checks: unplug (not just switch off) everything on the tripping circuit for a day — trips stopping means an appliance; then reintroduce half at a time. Keep a log of trip times against weather and appliance use. If it trips with everything unplugged, the RCD or the wiring is damaged.

Decision point: the unplug-and-log process is yours and genuinely diagnostic. After that it's an electrician with an insulation tester and an RCD tester — and document everything for a possible insurance claim, since storm damage to fixed wiring and appliances is often covered. Don't keep resetting and living with it: intermittent leakage after a surge is a fault announcing itself.
The outlet by my desk sometimes cuts power to my monitor for a second when I plug in or unplug anything from the other socket of the same double outlet. The monitor's fine. What's loose?

The giveaway is the mechanical link: disturbing one socket interrupts the other. On a double outlet both sockets share internal connections and the incoming cable terminates in the same box, so causes in order: (1) a loose terminal inside the outlet — the act of plugging in flexes the unit and momentarily breaks a marginal connection; (2) the outlet's internal contacts or bus links worn so vibration breaks continuity; (3) a loose plug on the monitor side — ruled partly by your test, since the trigger is the OTHER socket, but check the monitor's plug pins are tight in their own right.

Discriminating checks: plug a lamp into the monitor's socket and wiggle the neighbouring plug — lamp flicker confirms the outlet, not the monitor. Try the monitor in a different outlet for a day to fully clear it. Stop the wiggle-testing quickly though: a loose connection under load arcs, and arcing is what turns a loose terminal into a burnt one.

Decision point: this outlet needs opening, which means breaker off and proving dead, or an electrician. The usual finding is a conductor that was never fully home under its screw, now heat-cycled loose; the fix is re-terminating on clean copper or replacing the outlet. Don't keep using it for the monitor meanwhile — repeated micro-interruptions are unkind to electronics and the arcing risk grows each time.
Our fridge is too warm — milk is going off early — but the freezer compartment is still properly cold. It's a combined fridge-freezer with one compressor. How can one half work and not the other?

Because in most fridge-freezers the compressor only cools the freezer directly; the fridge is cooled by cold air bled from the freezer through a duct, controlled by a damper. So a warm fridge with a cold freezer means the cold exists but isn't reaching or circulating in the fridge. Causes in order: (1) the evaporator fan failing or iced up — it pushes the cold air around; if it stops, the freezer (wrapped around the coil) stays cold while the fridge starves; listen for the fan with the door switch pressed in — silence is suspicious; (2) the air duct between the compartments blocked by ice or by food stacked against the vents; (3) the damper stuck closed; (4) the fridge's own door seal leaking warm air faster than the modest cold supply can cope.

Discriminating checks: feel for cold air movement at the fridge's internal vents with the door switch held; clear anything stacked against the vents; check the door seal with a banknote — it should drag when pulled out of the closed door, all the way round. If you hear the fan straining or grinding, or see heavy frost on the freezer's back panel, ice is strangling the airflow.

Decision point: clearing vents, seal checks, and a full 24-hour manual defrost (empty, doors open) are DIY and cure the ice cases. A dead fan motor or damper is a repair-technician job on most models — and anything on the sealed refrigerant side always is.

The washing machine finishes its cycle with the drum still full of water, and the clothes are sodden. It drains fine if I run a drain programme after restarting it... sometimes. What's the usual culprit?

Intermittent failure to drain, sometimes cured by a restart, narrows it well. Causes in order: (1) a partially blocked pump filter — the coin trap at the front bottom of most machines fills with coins, hair grips, and lint until the pump can only sometimes push past it; the single commonest cause of this exact symptom; (2) a kinked or slime-restricted drain hose, or a house drain connection (the standpipe/spigot) partly blocked with detergent sludge; (3) a pump impeller worn or obstructed by a small object that shifts position — which fits the 'sometimes' behaviour beautifully.

Discriminating checks: put a shallow tray down, open the pump filter flap, and unscrew the filter slowly (expect up to a litre of water). Debris in the filter and a free-spinning impeller you can flick with a finger usually ends the diagnosis. If the filter is clean, detach the drain hose at the house connection and run a drain cycle into a bucket: strong flow into the bucket means the house side is blocked; weak flow means the machine side (pump/hose) is.

Decision point: filter cleaning and hose checks are standard owner maintenance — do them before any callout. A dead pump is a moderately priced part swap; whether that's DIY depends on your comfort opening the machine (unplugged, water everywhere) — a repair technician is the safe default.

Our tumble dryer tumbles and blows, but the air is cold and clothes come out damp after a full cycle. It heats if I run it empty on the hottest setting... no wait, it doesn't. No heat at all. Where's the fault likely to be?

Tumbling with airflow but zero heat means the motor, belt, and fan are proven good by observation, and the fault is confined to the heating circuit. Causes in order: (1) a tripped thermal cut-out (one-shot thermostat) — dryers have safety stats that open permanently or semi-permanently when the machine overheats, and they overheat when airflow is poor: a choked lint filter or blocked vent hose is usually the upstream cause; (2) a failed heating element — an open circuit in the coil; (3) a cycling thermostat or control fault.

Discriminating checks: first, the airflow story — pull the lint filter (is it filmed over with a grey mat that water would bead on?), and check the vent hose and outside vent flap for lint dams. Run the dryer and look at the outside vent: strong warm... in your case strong cool airflow confirms air moves but isn't heated. On many models the cut-out has a small reset button on the back panel or near the heater housing — if yours does and it clicks, you've found it, but it tripped for a reason (see airflow).

Decision point: filters, hoses, and a manufacturer-provided reset button are owner jobs. Element and thermostat testing needs the back off and a multimeter on mains components — repair technician territory for most people. And fix the airflow cause, or the new cut-out will trip again within weeks.
Our dishwasher runs and drains, but glasses come out with gritty specks stuck on them and there's sandy residue in the bottom of the tub. The filter looks clean. What am I missing?

Grit redeposited on glassware means dirty water is being sprayed back onto the load — the machine is washing with its own soil. A clean-looking filter is the trap: the filter may be clean while the spray path is not. Causes in order: (1) the filter actually mis-seated or a mesh torn, letting food particles recirculate — 'looks clean' isn't the same as 'sealing and intact'; (2) spray arm jets blocked with limescale or seeds, so arms barely rotate and jets dribble instead of blasting — check by spinning them by hand and poking jets clear; (3) the sump below the filter full of accumulated sludge that the wash water churns through; (4) water too cool because the heater is failing, so grease stays mobile and resettles as grit with food particles.

Discriminating checks: after a cycle, is the water in the sump area (under the filter) gritty? Run the machine empty on the hottest programme with a dishwasher cleaner and inspect the next load. Mark a spray arm's position, run two minutes, open and see if it moved — a stationary arm means no rotation.

Decision point: filters, spray arms, and sump cleaning are owner maintenance with gloves on. If grit persists with a spotless interior and rotating arms, suspect the heater or circulation pump — technician. Also check your rinse-aid and salt settings if you're in a hard-water area: scale grit and food grit look similar but the fix differs.
Our oven heats up but takes twice as long as it should to reach temperature, and cakes bake unevenly — done at the back, pale at the front. It's a fan oven, about eight years old. What's degrading?

A fan oven that's slow to heat and uneven front-to-back points at the fan system and the element working as a pair. Causes in order: (1) the fan motor failing or running slowly — in a fan oven the element rings the fan, and without vigorous airflow the heat stratifies: the back near the element overcooks while the front lags, exactly your pattern; listen — a healthy fan is a steady whoosh, a dying one is slow, noisy, or starts late; (2) the circular element partially failed — these elements can lose a section and still glow, delivering half power, which explains slow preheat with some heat; (3) a door seal perished, leaking heat at the front — that also biases pale-at-front.

Discriminating checks: watch through the glass — does the fan spin up promptly and fast when the oven is on? Check the seal: close the door on a banknote at several points; loose at the front bottom is a leak. An oven thermometer in the centre tells you whether the set temperature is even reached eventually (slow but accurate = power/airflow; never reaches = element/thermostat).

Decision point: door seals are a pull-off, push-on owner part. Fan motors and elements are inside the back panel among mains terminals — a repair technician unless you're genuinely competent with appliances unplugged and tested dead. Don't just compensate with longer cooking: a failing fan makes the element overheat locally and shortens its life too.
Our gas hob lights fine but one burner keeps going out a few seconds after I release the knob. The other three hold. Is this something I can fix?

Mostly no — and the part that makes it tempting is also the part that makes it professional work. That burner has a flame-failure device: a thermocouple sits in the flame, generates a tiny voltage that holds the gas valve open, and if the flame dies the gas shuts. Your symptom — lights while you hold the knob (you're manually holding the valve open), dies when released — means the safety chain isn't sustaining: causes in order: (1) the thermocouple is dirty, mispositioned, or failed — the flame isn't bathing its tip, often because the burner cap is slightly mis-seated or the thermocouple has aged out; (2) the burner ports are partly blocked so the flame is small or lopsided at the thermocouple's position; (3) the valve's electromagnetic unit failing.

What you may safely do: lift off the burner cap and rings, check they're seated flat and the ports are clean (a soft brush, no poking wires into jets), and relight. If the cap was askew, that can genuinely cure it.

Decision point: beyond reseating and surface cleaning, stop. Thermocouples and gas valves are gas work — in the UK that's Gas Safe registered engineers only, and the same logic applies anywhere: a fault in the device whose entire job is preventing unburned gas release must never be bypassed, taped down, or 'held open' with a weight on the knob. Book the engineer; it's a cheap part and a short visit.
