The fridge has started running almost constantly and there's a band of frost building on the inside back wall. Food near the back sometimes freezes. It's frost-free, supposedly. What's going wrong?

A 'frost-free' fridge with frost building inside and a compressor that rarely rests has an air-management problem. Causes in order: (1) a door seal leaking — moist room air enters continuously, its water freezes on the cold back wall (the evaporator's location shows through), and the compressor runs forever fighting the warm leak; the seal is the first suspect whenever frost appears in a frost-free cabinet; (2) the door being left fractionally ajar by a shelf or bottle — same mechanism, free fix; (3) the defrost system failing (heater, timer, or sensor) so the evaporator ices progressively — but that usually shows frost in the freezer and rising temperatures, whereas your food is over-cooling at the back, which fits air leak better.

Discriminating checks: the banknote test around the door seal — drag should be firm everywhere; a section with no grip is the leak. Look for a frost pattern concentrated near one corner or edge, which maps to the leak's location. Check nothing inside pushes the door. Clean the seal's folds — crumbs and slime hold them open.

Decision point: reseating contents, cleaning or replacing a push-in seal, and levelling the fridge so the door self-closes are DIY. If the seal tests perfectly and frost still grows within a week, the defrost system is at fault — technician, since it needs panels off and component testing.

Our front-load washer vibrates violently and walks across the floor on the spin cycle, but only with big loads like towels. Small loads are fine. It didn't do this when it was installed two years ago.

Load-dependent violent vibration that developed over time has mechanical causes, and 'only big loads' is informative: a heavy, waterlogged towel load is the hardest test of the suspension and balance systems. Causes in order: (1) worn suspension dampers (the shock absorbers holding the drum tub) — two years is early but they do fail, and worn dampers show exactly this: fine when lightly loaded, wild when the mass grows; (2) the machine no longer level or a levelling foot wound loose — check for rocking when you push a top corner; (3) transit bolts never removed — but that would have shaken from day one, so your 'didn't do it when installed' rules it out; (4) a cracked drum spider or failing bearing — usually accompanied by noise, a rumble or knocking on spin, and play when you lift the drum.

Discriminating checks: rock test for level; press down on the drum through the door seal and let go — it should settle in one or two bounces, not bounce repeatedly (dampers). Spin the empty drum by hand: smooth and silent is good; rumble or roughness is bearings. Lift the drum at the top of the door opening — clunking play means bearing/spider trouble.

Decision point: levelling feet are yours. Dampers are a moderately involved part swap; bearings/spider are major surgery — for most people that's a technician's quote weighed against the machine's age and value.
The microwave runs, the turntable spins, the light works — but food stays stone cold. It happened suddenly yesterday. Any hope, or is it dead?

Sudden total loss of heating with everything else working means the microwave-generating side has failed while the control and motor side lives. In order: (1) a failed magnetron (the tube that makes the microwaves) — the commonest cause of this exact picture; (2) the high-voltage diode or capacitor failing, which starves the magnetron; (3) a door interlock switch fault — usually that stops it running at all, but a partially failed switch can let the fan and light run without enabling the magnetron circuit; (4) the high-voltage fuse, fitted on some models, blown by any of the above.

The honest advice: there is no safe owner-level check beyond confirming the power settings aren't at zero and trying a cup of water for two minutes to be sure. The high-voltage capacitor inside a microwave can hold a lethal charge for days after unplugging — microwaves are the one household appliance where 'just look inside' can kill a healthy adult.

Decision point: technician or replacement, full stop — and with magnetron-age machines, replacement usually wins on cost. Don't run it empty 'to test', don't bypass door switches, and don't let anyone enthusiastic open the case. This is a hard safety boundary, not a lack of ambition.
Our kettle has started switching itself off long before the water boils, then after a minute it will go again and finish. Descaling helped for a week. What's wearing out?

Early cut-off that recovers after a pause is a thermostat story: the kettle's control thinks boiling has happened, or its safety cut-out trips, then resets as it cools. Causes in order: (1) scale on the temperature sensor or the concealed element plate — scale insulates, so the sensor's local temperature overshoots while the bulk water is still cool; your descaling helping for a week strongly supports scale as at least a contributor, and if your water is hard it re-forms fast; (2) the steam switch/thermostat itself fatiguing — the bimetal disc that flips at boiling weakens with thousands of cycles and starts flipping early; (3) a poor contact in the base connector making intermittent power — but that would show flickering lights and erratic behaviour rather than a clean early 'click' off.

Discriminating checks: descale thoroughly with citric acid, filling only to the sensor area, and test with the lid open vs closed — the steam switch needs steam channelled to it; a kettle that only cuts early with the lid properly shut is behaving differently from one that does it always. Note whether the switch-off click sounds at the same water temperature each time (thermostat) or randomly (contact).

Decision point: descaling is the whole DIY repertoire — kettle internals and bases are sealed mains assemblies with no user parts. A fatigued thermostat means a new kettle; they're inexpensive, and a kettle that can't be trusted to boil is also one whose boil-dry protection you shouldn't test.
The dishwasher tablet isn't dissolving properly — I find a mushy half-tablet in the dispenser or on the tub floor after the wash, and cleaning is poor. What decides whether a tablet dissolves?

A tablet needs three things: the dispenser door opening at the right time, hot water, and spray actually hitting it. Your symptom splits along those lines. Causes in order: (1) the dispenser door obstructed — a tall plate or chopping board in front of it is the classic; the door can't flip open, the tablet slumps out late into cool water; (2) the dispenser latch/spring failing so it opens late or not at all; (3) water not getting hot (heater fault) — tablets dissolve slowly in lukewarm water, and poor cleaning follows; (4) low water pressure/fill or blocked spray arm reducing the water action on the tablet.

Discriminating checks: load the machine leaving clear space in front of the dispenser and run again — cheapest test in this whole list. Test the door by hand: it should spring open smartly when the latch is released. Run the hottest programme and open mid-cycle (carefully) — the water should be too hot to hold your hand in; merely warm water convicts the heater.

Decision point: loading changes and dispenser cleaning (old tablet residue gums the latch — scrub it) are yours. Heater or latch-mechanism replacement is technician work inside the door and tub. If the tablet dissolves fine loose in the cutlery basket on a hot wash, you've confirmed the dispenser path is the fault, which is useful information to hand over.

Our freezer is cold but the high-temperature alarm keeps sounding, and the compressor seems to run in long cycles. A thermometer inside reads -15°C, and I know freezers should be about -18°C. What's marginal here?

Your thermometer has done the key measurement: -15°C instead of -18°C is a system working at maybe 80% — cold enough to feel cold, not cold enough to be right. Causes in order: (1) the condenser coils (underneath or at the back) clogged with dust — the freezer can't reject heat efficiently, so it runs long and still falls a few degrees short; this is the most likely and the most fixable; (2) the door seal leaking or the door opened constantly, adding heat load; (3) the evaporator fan weak or the evaporator icing (defrost fault) reducing cooling capacity; (4) refrigerant slightly low from a micro-leak — last, and not owner-touchable.

Discriminating checks: pull the freezer out and look at the coils — a felt of dust is a confession. Vacuum/brush them clean (unplugged), restore airflow clearance at the back, and re-measure after 12 hours: back to -18 convicts the coils. Banknote-test the seal. Listen for the internal fan running whenever the compressor does.

Decision point: coil cleaning and seals are owner jobs and cure most marginal freezers. If spotless coils and a sound seal still leave you at -15, the fault is in the defrost/fan/refrigerant world — technician. Meanwhile, -15 keeps food safe for days-to-weeks rather than months; eat the ice cream first and don't refreeze anything that has thawed.
Our coffee machine has gone slow — it drips instead of flowing, the coffee tastes weak, and it gurgles and spits steam near the end. It's two years old and we've never descaled it. Related?

Almost certainly all one cause: limescale. Two years of hard water deposits scale in the boiler and, critically, in the narrow pipes and shower screen the water must pass through. Restricted flow explains the dripping pace; water spending too long in contact — yet channelled through gaps in a scaled group head — explains weak extraction; and the gurgling/steam is water flashing to vapour in overheated narrow passages instead of flowing freely. The three symptoms arriving together on a never-descaled machine is about as clean a diagnosis as appliances give.

The fix is the diagnosis confirmed: run a proper descale cycle with citric acid or a manufacturer descaler, following the machine's procedure, and repeat it if the first pass brings out a lot of debris. Flow returning to normal over one or two cycles confirms scale was the whole story.

Decision point: descaling is routine owner maintenance — no callout needed. Escalate only if flow stays poor after two thorough descales, which moves suspicion to a failing pump (weak pressure) or a perished group seal, and those are repair-shop jobs. And descale on a schedule from now on; scale left long enough eventually blocks a passage completely and overheats the boiler.
The spin dryer function of our washer-dryer leaves clothes much wetter than the old separate washer did, even on the highest spin speed setting. Is it faulty, or is something else different?

Probably not faulty — but verify rather than assume, because two real faults mimic it. The physics first: extraction depends on actual drum RPM sustained, drum diameter, and spin duration; many washer-dryers spin slower in practice than their badge speed (the rating is often the washer-only model's figure), and their smaller drums hold the load against the wall less effectively. Causes to rule out in order: (1) the machine reducing spin speed automatically because the load is unbalanced — modern machines detect a lopsided load and cap the spin to protect themselves, so a single heavy item (a bath mat, one pair of jeans) can leave everything wet; (2) a partially blocked pump filter slowing drainage, so clothes sit in residual water during spin; (3) genuinely slower drum speed from a worn belt or motor issue — listen for the pitch of a full-speed spin.

Discriminating checks: run a spin-only cycle with a small, evenly distributed load of already-washed items and weigh the load before and after (a luggage scale on the basket works): good extraction on a balanced load clears the machine. Clean the pump filter regardless.

Decision point: load habits and filter are yours. If a balanced small load still comes out dripping and the spin sounds lazy, that's a technician — belt, motor, or control. If balanced loads extract well, the machine is honest and the old one was simply stronger.

There's a buzzing from our fridge every few minutes followed by a click, and then silence — and the fridge has stopped cooling altogether since this morning. The light inside works. What are those sounds telling me?

That buzz-click cycle is the compressor trying to start, failing, and being cut off by its overload protector — repeatedly. The light working proves mains reaches the fridge; the cooling system is failing to start. Causes in order: (1) a failed start relay (the small device that gives the compressor its starting boost) — the commonest and cheapest cause, and its failure produces exactly this buzz-click rhythm; (2) a failed start capacitor on models that have one; (3) the compressor itself seized or with a burnt winding — it hums, draws heavy current, overheats, and the protector clicks it off; (4) the overload protector itself failed weak.

Discriminating checks: unplug, wait, and locate the relay on the compressor's side (behind the rear lower panel) — a relay that rattles like a castanet when shaken has literally fallen apart inside and is convicted. Burnt smell at the compressor terminals also points deeper than the relay.

Decision point: a like-for-like relay swap is a known confident-DIY part (unplugged, photograph the wiring first), and it's cheap enough to try before condemning the compressor. If a new relay still buzzes and clicks, the compressor is done — that's sealed-system work, a technician's quote, and often the point where replacement wins. Meanwhile keep the door shut: a full, closed fridge buys you hours of safe food temperatures.
Our oven's temperature is wildly off — set to 200°C, an oven thermometer reads 160°C, and food undercooks. But the thermostat light cycles on and off as if it's regulating happily. Where's the lie?

The cycling light tells you the control loop is working — it's switching the element on a sensor's say-so. So the lie is in one of two places: the sensor reports the wrong temperature (the oven believes it's at 200 when it's at 160), or the sensor is right but the element can't deliver full heat. Causes in order: (1) a drifting temperature sensor/thermostat — sensors age and read low-resistance/high-temperature falsely, so the oven cuts off early, satisfied and wrong; a consistent 40° shortfall that the control is serenely unaware of fits this best; (2) a partially failed element delivering reduced power — but then the oven would usually run the element almost constantly and still fall short, and your light cycles normally, which argues the control thinks it has arrived; (3) the thermometer's placement — verify it hangs in the centre, not touching a wall or shelf.

Discriminating checks: re-test with the thermometer centred and the oven given a full 30 minutes to stabilise; test at a second setpoint (150°C) — a proportional error at both suggests sensor drift; an error only at high heat suggests power. Swap in a second cheap thermometer to clear the instrument itself.

Decision point: sensor replacement is a modest part — on many ovens it unclips inside the cavity — but it sits among mains connections, so technician for most. Hand them your two-setpoint measurements: 'reads 40 low at both 150 and 200 with centred thermometers' turns a vague complaint into a confirmed sensor job.
The washing machine smells musty and the smell transfers to clean laundry. The drum looks clean. Where does the smell actually live in these machines?

In a front-loader the smell rarely lives in the drum you can see — it lives in the wet, warm, nutrient-rich places you can't: (1) the door seal's folds, which hold a film of water, detergent residue, and skin cells — pull the folds back and you'll usually find black mould and slime, the number-one source; (2) the detergent drawer and its housing, where undissolved powder and fabric softener feed mould; (3) a biofilm inside the sump and hoses from constant low-temperature washes — 30-40°C cycles never kill it, and modern detergents at low doses leave residue it feeds on; (4) the pump filter area, holding stagnant water.

Discriminating checks: the seal folds and the drawer are a look-and-sniff test — if both are clean and the smell persists, it's the internal biofilm, proven by the smell being worst on the first wash after the machine sits idle.

Fix path, all owner-level: scrub the seal folds and drawer with hot water and a cloth (a diluted bleach wipe for mould, gloves on), clean the filter, then run the hottest empty cycle with a washing-machine cleaner or a cup of soda crystals. Prevent recurrence: leave the door and drawer ajar between washes, wipe the seal dry, and run a hot maintenance wash monthly. No technician needed unless the smell survives two deep cleans — then suspect a perished seal harbouring mould inside its layers, which is a replaceable part.
Our chest freezer in the garage stopped working during a cold snap — the garage got down to about -5°C. It started working again when the weather warmed. Is the freezer faulty?

Probably not faulty — you've met a known quirk of how many freezers (and especially fridge-freezers) are controlled. A freezer's thermostat senses temperature and runs the compressor when cooling is needed. In a very cold garage, two things can go wrong: (1) on fridge-freezers with a single thermostat located in the fridge section, if the garage air is already near fridge temperature, the thermostat never calls for cooling — so the freezer section, which depends on that same compressor, warms up and thaws; (2) on plain freezers, thick cold oil and a sluggish thermostat in deep cold can delay starts, and many appliances are rated for a minimum ambient (their 'climate class', often +10°C or +16°C) below which operation isn't guaranteed.

Discriminating checks: read the rating plate's climate class — if your garage went below it, the freezer behaved as designed, not as broken. Note whether food actually thawed (freezer contents warming = the single-thermostat trap) or the unit merely rested while contents stayed frozen (harmless).

Decision point: no repair needed if it's the ambient trap. The cures are environmental: move the freezer indoors, warm the garage space near it, or replace with a model explicitly rated for garage/outbuilding use (some are built for sub-zero ambients). Don't let anyone sell you a compressor for a climate-class problem — check the plate first, it's free.
My car makes a single loud click when I turn the key and nothing else happens. The dashboard lights come on bright. What does that one click tell me?

A single solid click with bright dash lights is a specific and useful symptom. The click is the starter solenoid engaging — so the key switch, the wiring to the starter, and enough battery voltage to work the solenoid are all proven. What isn't happening is the starter motor turning the engine. Causes in order: (1) the solenoid's main contacts are burnt — it clicks but doesn't pass the heavy current to the motor; a classic failure; (2) the starter motor itself failed (worn brushes, dead spot on the commutator — sometimes a sharp tap on the starter body with a wrench jolts it back for one start, which is a diagnostic as much as a trick); (3) a poor heavy-cable connection at the battery or starter — enough contact for lights and solenoid, not enough for 200 amps of cranking; check for corrosion and looseness first because it's free.

Discriminating checks: clean and tighten the battery terminals, then try again. Have someone turn the key while you listen at the starter: click at the starter confirms the solenoid. Headlights on while trying: if they stay bright during the click, the battery isn't collapsing — pointing harder at the starter/solenoid than the battery.

Decision point: terminal cleaning is yours. Starter replacement is a mechanic job for most (access, heavy cables, sometimes exhaust in the way) — and don't keep clicking away; each attempt arcs the contacts further.
When I turn the key I get a rapid-fire clicking — clickclickclickclick — and the dash lights flicker with it. The car was fine yesterday. Battery or starter?

That machine-gun clicking is the battery's signature, not the starter's. Here's the mechanism: the battery has enough charge to engage the starter solenoid, but the moment the starter draws its heavy current, the voltage collapses, the solenoid drops out, the load vanishes, voltage recovers — and the cycle repeats several times a second. A healthy starter on a dead battery makes this noise; a failed starter almost never does. Causes in order: (1) a discharged battery — lights or an interior light left on, a boot/trunk light stuck on, or short trips in cold weather; (2) a battery at end of life that can no longer deliver cranking current even though it shows 12 volts at rest; (3) corroded terminals creating the same collapse at the connection.

Discriminating checks: clean the terminals first (free). Jump-start it: if it starts instantly on jump power, the starter is innocent and the battery/charging story is everything. Then the real question becomes why it's flat — after a full charge (or a 30-minute drive), does it start tomorrow morning? A battery that won't hold overnight charge after being charged is either being drained by something or is finished; most auto parts shops will load-test it free.

Decision point: jump-starting, terminal cleaning, and a battery swap are owner-level on most cars. If a new, charged battery goes flat repeatedly, the fault is a parasitic drain or charging problem — that's a mechanic with a multimeter, not another battery.
My car cranks strongly and normally but just won't fire — it turns over and over without catching. It ran fine when I parked it last night. What systems should I be thinking about?

Strong cranking rules out the battery and starter in one stroke: the engine is spinning but missing one of its three requirements — fuel, spark, or compression/timing. On a modern car, in rough probability order for a sudden overnight failure: (1) fuel delivery — a failed fuel pump (listen at the filler cap or under the rear seat when someone turns the key to ON: a healthy pump hums for two seconds to prime; silence is telling), an empty tank despite the gauge (gauges lie when a sender sticks), or a tripped inertia switch after a knock; (2) the immobiliser not recognising the key — watch for a flashing key/security light on the dash while cranking; try the spare key, it's a free test; (3) a failed crankshaft position sensor — the ECU won't fire injectors or plugs if it can't see the engine turning; this is a very common sudden no-start with strong crank; (4) flooded engine if there were several short start attempts.

Discriminating checks: pump prime hum, spare key, security light behaviour, and confirm actual fuel in the tank. Note whether it almost-catches (suggests fuel weak/flooding) or turns over dead-flat (suggests no spark/no injection at all).

Decision point: key and listening tests are yours, and don't crank endlessly — you'll flatten the battery and flood it. Beyond that this is a mechanic with a diagnostic scanner; the sensor and pump are both 'parts cannon' guesses without fault codes and a fuel-pressure test.
My brakes squeal when I brake gently in town, but they're quiet under hard braking, and stopping power feels normal. The pads were replaced about a year ago. Should I be worried?

A light-braking squeal that's absent under hard braking and doesn't affect stopping is usually vibration, not danger — but it deserves one inspection to separate the harmless causes from the one that matters. Causes in order: (1) pad vibration/glazing: at light pressure the pads chatter microscopically against the disc; harder pressure clamps the chatter silent. Glazed pads or missing anti-squeal shims from the replacement fit this; (2) the wear indicators — thin metal tabs designed to squeal as a warning — but those usually announce themselves as pads approach end of life, and yours are a year old (mileage matters more than time, though); (3) surface rust or embedded grit after wet weather, which typically clears after a few stops.

Discriminating checks: look through the wheel spokes at the pad thickness if visible — plenty of meat argues against wear tabs. Note whether the squeal appears only for the first few stops of the day (rust film) or all day (vibration). A quiet road test with windows down, braking lightly past a wall, helps locate which wheel.

Decision point: this is an inspection, not an emergency — but brakes are a hard line: any grinding, pulling, pedal change, or visible thin pads means a mechanic promptly, and pad/shim/disc work is mechanic work for most people. Don't let anyone sell you discs and pads on the phone; the squeal pattern you describe most often ends with shims, a clean, or nothing at all.
There's a grinding noise when I brake now, and the pedal feels slightly rough through my foot. It started as a squeak last month that I ignored. How urgent is this, honestly?

Urgent — today, not this week, and drive as little as possible in between, ideally straight to a mechanic. The story you've told is the textbook progression: the squeak last month was almost certainly the wear indicators announcing the pads were nearly finished; the grinding now is what happens after the friction material is gone — the steel backing plate of the pad is braking directly against the disc. The roughness through the pedal is that metal-on-metal contact transmitting vibration. Every stop now is machining your discs thinner, and stopping distances lengthen as the plate overheats and glazes the disc surface.

What to do: no diagnosis is needed and no home check adds anything — the symptom combination is conclusive. Book the mechanic, drive gently and directly there (leave big gaps, brake early and lightly), or have it recovered if the pedal feels very long, the car pulls hard to one side, or braking feels seriously weak — those mean the braking is compromised enough that driving it is a risk to others, not just to your discs.

Decision point: this is entirely professional work — pads certainly, discs almost certainly (they'll be scored and possibly below minimum thickness), and the calipers need checking for the seizure that sometimes caused the uneven wear in the first place. The expensive lesson in the story: the squeak was the cheap warning; grinding is the expensive one.
My steering wheel vibrates between about 60 and 70 mph but is smooth below that and smooths out again above 75. Around town there's nothing. What's speed-specific like that?

A vibration that lives in a narrow speed band and vanishes either side is a resonance — something rotating is out of balance, and at 60-70 its frequency matches the steering/suspension's natural frequency. Causes in order: (1) front wheel imbalance — a thrown balance weight is the classic; front wheels because you feel it through the wheel (rear imbalance is felt through the seat instead — a useful discriminator); (2) a tyre defect — a bulge, flat spot, or internal belt separation that only shows its effect at speed; (3) a bent rim from a pothole; (4) worn suspension joints — these usually add looseness and noise at other times too, so they're lower on the list for a purely band-limited symptom.

Discriminating checks: look at the front tyres closely — bulges in the sidewall (that tyre is unsafe, full stop), uneven wear, a missing weight's clean rectangle on the rim. The decisive test is cheap: have the front wheels balanced and ask the shop to spin them and watch for run-out — a balancing machine exposes imbalance, a bent rim, and a separating tyre in one go.

Decision point: visual tyre checks are yours, and a sidewall bulge means don't drive on it beyond getting to a tyre shop slowly. Balancing and tyres are tyre-shop work; if balance is perfect and the band persists, then it's a mechanic for joints, bearings, and driveshafts. Don't just drive at 75 to avoid it — a separating tyre fails at speed.

The whole car shudders when it's idling at lights — the revs look normal and steady — but it drives perfectly smoothly once moving. Engine mounts were mentioned by a friend. How do I test that theory?

Your friend's theory is testable and plausible, but split the symptom first: an engine that RUNS rough at idle (misfiring) also shudders, and mounts only transmit or damp vibration — they don't create it. Discriminators: (1) if the rev counter is truly steady and the engine note sounds even, the engine is probably running cleanly and the shudder is its normal idle vibration reaching the cabin through a collapsed or hardened rubber mount — mounts perish with age and heat, the rubber cracks or the mount sags so metal meets metal; (2) if there's any unevenness — a putt-putt in the exhaust note, a tremor in the rev needle — that's a misfire (plug, coil, injector) and mounts are innocent bystanders.

Discriminating checks: watch the engine while a helper shifts between Drive and Reverse with the brake held (stand to the side, never in front): a worn mount lets the engine rock dramatically and clunk as torque reverses. Inspect mounts visually for cracked, oil-soaked, or collapsed rubber. In gear vs in neutral: shudder much worse in Drive at a stop is typical of mount trouble under load.

Decision point: observation is yours and worth doing before any garage visit. Mount replacement is a mechanic job (engine support, lifting, torque settings). If the evidence says misfire instead — uneven note, flashing engine light ever — that's also a mechanic, but a different one conversation: plugs and coils, not rubber.

My car needed a jump start twice this month. Both times it had sat for two days. Once running, it's fine, and the battery was new last year. How do I work out whether it's the battery, the alternator, or something draining it?

Use the timing, because each suspect has a different alibi pattern. The alternator charges while you drive; if it were failing, the car would tend to die or dim WHILE driving, or need jumps after drives, not specifically after sitting. A battery that self-discharges or is drained by a parasitic load fails exactly as yours does: fine in daily use (the alternator keeps topping it), dead after two days parked. Causes in order: (1) a parasitic drain — a module not sleeping, a boot or glovebox light staying on, an aftermarket accessory wired live; (2) the battery itself — 'new last year' lowers but doesn't eliminate this; a battery can be killed early by a few deep discharges, in a vicious circle with the drain; (3) alternator diode failure, which can BOTH undercharge and drain the battery overnight — the one alternator fault that fits your pattern.

Discriminating checks: charge the battery fully, then disconnect the negative terminal overnight (or for two days if you can spare the car): if it starts happily after sitting disconnected, the battery holds charge and something in the car is drinking it — drain confirmed. If it's flat even disconnected, the battery is done. A parts shop can load-test it free.

Decision point: the disconnect test and visual checks (lights left on, dashcam hardwired?) are yours. Finding a drain means measuring current draw fuse by fuse with the car asleep — a mechanic/auto-electrician job, and hand them your disconnect-test result; it halves their work.
There's a whining noise from the engine that rises and falls with the revs, even when the car is stationary. It started gradually over the last few weeks. Belts? Bearings? How do I narrow it down?

A whine that tracks engine revs with the car stationary eliminates everything downstream of the engine — gearbox, wheels, road noise — and points at the engine's rotating accessories or the belt driving them. Causes in order: (1) a failing bearing in one of the belt-driven accessories — alternator, power steering pump, AC compressor, idler or tensioner pulley; worn bearings whine before they rumble; (2) low power steering fluid making the pump whine — check this first if you have hydraulic steering, because it's a two-minute look and the whine characteristically changes when you turn the wheel; (3) the belt itself — a glazed or contaminated belt usually squeals rather than whines, and pitch follows revs too.

Discriminating checks: steering test at idle — whine swelling as you turn the wheel convicts the steering pump/fluid. AC on vs off: whine changing with the compressor clutch engaging points at the compressor or its pulley. A mechanic's stethoscope (or a long screwdriver, handle to ear, tip on each accessory — carefully, away from the moving belt) localises the loudest bearing.

Decision point: fluid level check and the AC/steering listening tests are yours. Belt-off component testing and any pulley/alternator replacement is a mechanic — belts under tension and spinning accessories punish careless fingers. Don't ignore a growing whine: a bearing that seizes can throw the belt, and losing the belt means losing steering assistance, charging, and often cooling in one moment.
My car pulls to the left under braking but tracks straight when I'm just driving. Tyre pressures are equal. What makes a car pull only when braking?

Pulling only under braking means the braking forces are unequal left-to-right — the car yaws toward the side that brakes harder (or away from the side that barely brakes). Tracking straight at cruise clears alignment and most tyre causes from suspicion. Causes in order: (1) a seized or sticking caliper on one side — most often the RIGHT caliper underperforming (its pads barely squeeze), so the left side does the work and the car dives left; the seized one can also stick ON, dragging; (2) a contaminated or glazed pad on one side (oil/grease from a leaking seal ruins friction); (3) a collapsed flexible brake hose internally — it can act as a one-way valve, delaying pressure to one caliper; (4) badly mismatched pad wear side to side.

Discriminating checks: after a drive with several stops, carefully compare front wheel temperatures (an infrared thermometer is ideal; a cautious hand near — not on — each wheel works): the lazier side runs cooler, a dragging side runs hot. Look for uneven pad thickness through the spokes and any difference in disc appearance (one shiny, one dull/rusty means one isn't working).

Decision point: temperature comparison is yours and it's the key evidence to hand over. The repair — caliper, pads in axle pairs, hoses, brake fluid — is mechanic work, full stop: brakes are hydraulics and safety-critical, and a pull under braking will only get worse. Drive gently and get it booked promptly; if the pull is violent or the pedal feels abnormal, don't drive it.
My temperature gauge has started creeping above the middle on motorway climbs, then it comes back down on the flat. Around town it's normal. The car's never actually overheated. What's marginal?

A cooling system that's adequate in town but marginal under sustained load is losing capacity somewhere — a climb demands maximum cooling, and a system at 90% copes everywhere except there. Causes in order: (1) a partially blocked radiator — internal scale/sediment or external debris (leaves, insects, bent fins) reducing its effective area; (2) a thermostat not opening fully, restricting flow exactly when flow matters most; (3) a weak water pump (eroded impeller) or a slipping belt; (4) the radiator fan not helping at low road speeds — less relevant at motorway pace, where ram air dominates, so its low ranking here is deliberate; (5) low coolant level — check first because it's free.

Discriminating checks: coolant level and condition in the expansion tank (rusty brown coolant hints at internal corrosion/blockage). After a climb, feel across the radiator (carefully, engine off) or use an infrared thermometer: cold patches map the blocked sections. Note whether turning the cabin heater to full hot brings the gauge down — the heater is a spare radiator, and if it rescues the temperature, circulation exists but radiator capacity is short.

Decision point: level checks and observations are yours, and never open a hot pressurised cap — that's a scalding mechanism, not a check. Thermostat and radiator work is mechanic territory for most, and don't let marginal become a warped head gasket by ignoring the trend: overheating an engine once, properly, is the expensive version of this fault.
There's a clunk from the front of the car when I go over speed bumps, and another clunk when I first brake after reversing. Two different clunks or one?

Possibly one worn component announcing itself two ways, or two separate wear items — the two triggers stress different things, so treat them as two clues. Over bumps, the suspension compresses and extends: clunks there come from (1) worn anti-roll bar drop links — the commonest bump-clunk in modern cars, a small cheap part; (2) worn strut top mounts or tired shock absorbers; (3) a worn ball joint or control-arm bush. The brake-after-reversing clunk is different physics: brake pads shifting in their caliper carrier as the direction of braking torque reverses — often just pad movement (annoying, usually harmless if pads are correctly fitted with their clips), but it can also be a caliper or carrier worn loose.

Discriminating checks: bounce each front corner by hand and listen; rock the wheel top-to-bottom and side-to-side (car on the ground tells less — a mechanic's lift tells more). Note whether the bump clunk happens with both wheels (bump straight-on) or only one wheel at a time (drive one side over a bump) — one-sided localises it.

Decision point: listening and localising is yours and makes the garage visit cheaper. Anything in this list is mechanic work — suspension is springs under load and steering geometry — and a ball joint, if that's what it is, is safety-critical: a failed one can drop a corner of the car. Book it in weeks, not months, and mention both clunks.
My car uses about a litre of oil every thousand miles. There are no drips on the driveway and no blue smoke that I can see. The dealer says it's 'within tolerance'. Where can oil go invisibly?

Oil has only three exits: it leaks out, it's burned, or it stays and you mis-measure. No drips and no visible smoke narrows it but doesn't close the case. In order: (1) burned in small quantities — a litre per thousand miles burned gradually produces smoke too faint to see from the driver's seat, especially with a catalyst cleaning it up; usual paths are worn valve stem seals (puff of smoke on start-up or after idling, then clear) or oil passing the piston rings under load (smoke on hard acceleration — have someone follow you and watch); (2) an external leak that only opens when hot and driving, blowing back onto the exhaust or undertray rather than dripping on your drive — look for wet grime on the engine's underside and a burnt-oil smell after drives; (3) the PCV (crankcase ventilation) valve failed, letting oil mist get drawn into the intake and burned — a cheap part that mimics engine wear.

Discriminating checks: the follower test for smoke under acceleration and on start-up; a torch inspection underneath for fresh wet oil; check the coolant for oil contamination and the oil filler cap for mayonnaise-like emulsion (which would suggest an internal coolant/oil mix — a different, more serious fault).

Decision point: watching, topping up with the correct grade, and keeping a consumption log is yours — and the log matters, because rising consumption is the real warning. The diagnosis between seals, rings, and PCV is a mechanic's (compression and leak-down tests). 'Within tolerance' is a warranty phrase, not a diagnosis: keep records.

The steering has developed a dead spot in the middle — I can wiggle the wheel a couple of inches before the car responds — and it feels vague on the motorway. It crept up over months. How serious is this?

Serious enough to book promptly: free play in steering is wear in the one system where slack translates directly into delayed control, and on the motorway that vagueness is the car wandering within the slack before it answers. Because it crept up gradually, it's wear, not sudden damage. Causes in order: (1) worn track rod ends or inner tie rods — the joints between the steering rack and the wheels, the commonest source of centre play; (2) wear in the rack itself; (3) a worn steering column universal joint or coupling; (4) — check before all of these, because it's free — tyre pressures and tyre condition: soft front tyres feel vague and unresponsive in a way that mimics play, though they don't create true free movement at the wheel.

Discriminating checks: with the engine off and wheels straight, rock the steering wheel gently through the dead zone while a helper watches the front wheels: if the wheels don't move during the wiggle, the play is real and upstream of them. The helper can also watch each joint while you rock — the joint where motion enters but doesn't leave is the worn one. Any clunk accompanying the play strengthens the joint-wear story.

Decision point: watching and tyre pressures are yours; everything else is a mechanic, soon. Steering joints are safety-critical, pressed and torqued parts, and the car needs an alignment afterwards. If the play suddenly increases, or a clunk becomes a knock over bumps, stop driving it beyond getting to the garage — a track rod end that separates takes steering away entirely.
My wipers smear and judder across the windscreen even with new blades fitted last month. The screen looks clean. What else causes this?

New blades misbehaving moves suspicion from the blades to what they run on and how they're pressed. Causes in order: (1) contamination on the glass — traffic film, wax from a car wash, tree sap, or silicone from a previous treatment: the blade hydroplanes on the film and chatters; 'looks clean' doesn't exclude an invisible wax layer, and car-wash wax is the classic; (2) the wiper arm spring weakened or the arm slightly twisted, so blade pressure is uneven or the blade's attack angle is wrong — a blade must flip over at each end of the sweep; if it doesn't flip, it drags on its edge and judders one way; (3) a worn linkage giving the arm play.

Discriminating checks: clean the glass properly with a dedicated glass cleaner or a vinegar solution and polish dry — if smearing vanishes, it was film. Watch the blade at the turn-around points: it should visibly flop to the other side; judder in only one direction of travel means it's failing to flip in that direction (arm angle). Lift the arm and feel its spring tension against a healthy car's if you can.

Decision point: all owner-level — glass decontamination, arm checks, even arm replacement is a clip-on part on most cars. Only a worn linkage/motor is a mechanic job. One caution: never bend an arm randomly to 'add pressure' — the attack angle matters more than force, and a bent arm makes both directions worse.

My car has started drifting to the right on a straight, flat road when I let go of the wheel, and the steering wheel sits slightly off-centre. This began after I hit a pothole hard last month. What did the pothole likely do?

A pothole impact followed by a pull and an off-centre wheel is alignment until proven otherwise — the impact bent or shifted something in the steering/suspension geometry by a small amount. In order: (1) the toe setting knocked out of adjustment — a tie rod or its adjustment shifted; toe error both pulls and chews tyre edges fast; (2) a bent component — a tie rod, control arm, or even the wheel rim itself; (3) a damaged tyre from the same impact — a belt separation can create a 'radial pull' that mimics alignment; the off-centre wheel supports geometry change more than tyre, but both came from the same bang.

Discriminating checks: inspect that corner's tyre for bulges (a bulge ends the debate — replace the tyre) and check the rim for a dent on its inner edge, where potholes bite. Look at the front tyres' tread wear after a few hundred miles: feathering across the tread means toe is wrong. The tyre-swap test separates tyre from geometry: swap the front wheels side to side — if the pull reverses or vanishes, a tyre is the cause; if it still pulls right, it's geometry.

Decision point: inspection is yours; the cure is a tyre shop/mechanic with an alignment rig, and ask them to inspect for bent parts BEFORE aligning — aligning a car with a bent arm just sets wrong geometry precisely. Don't delay: toe error can destroy a tyre in a few thousand miles, and the off-centre wheel tells you something physically moved.

The air conditioning in my car blows cold at motorway speed but goes warm and stuffy when I'm idling in traffic. It also gets cold again as soon as I start moving. What's speed-dependent in an AC system?

The condenser is. Your AC dumps the cabin's heat at the condenser in front of the radiator, and it can shed that heat two ways: ram air from the car's motion, or the electric radiator/condenser fan when stationary. Cold at speed but warm at idle is the classic signature of the fan side failing — at 60 mph the airflow does the fan's job and masks it. Causes in order: (1) the condenser/radiator fan not running — failed motor, blown fuse, failed relay, or a temperature/pressure switch fault; (2) the condenser fins blocked with debris — but that usually degrades both cases, not just idle; (3) refrigerant slightly low — again usually degrades everything, so it's third for this clean speed split.

Discriminating check, definitive and free: idle the car, AC on max, and look at the fan behind the radiator (careful — it can start without warning; look, don't reach). If it's not spinning while the AC compressor is engaged, you've found it. Also watch whether the engine temperature gauge creeps up in the same traffic — the same fan serves the engine, so a rising gauge at idle confirms fan failure and raises the stakes.

Decision point: fuses are owner-level (check the fan fuse/relay in the fusebox against the manual). Fan motors and switches are a mechanic/auto-electrician. And take the engine-temperature link seriously: if the gauge climbs at idle, this stopped being a comfort fault — it's an overheating risk in the next traffic jam.
There's a sweet smell in the cabin when the heater is on, the windscreen mists up on the inside with a greasy film, and my coolant level has been dropping slowly. Three separate problems?

Almost certainly one problem with three symptoms — and you've assembled the classic triad for a leaking heater matrix (the small radiator inside the dashboard that provides cabin heat). The logic locks together: the matrix carries engine coolant; a leak there drips coolant into the heater box; the fan blows its vapour into the cabin — hence the sweet smell (ethylene glycol's signature), the greasy misting that resists wiping on the inside of the screen, and the slow coolant loss with no drips under the car, because the leak evaporates or drips into the cabin/footwell instead.

Discriminating checks: feel the front footwell carpets for dampness and sniff them — sweet and damp convicts it. Check whether the misting happens only with heat on (matrix) or also with cold air (suggests a different water leak — door seals, blocked scuttle drains). A cooling-system pressure test at a garage confirms the leak rate, though it can't see the matrix directly.

Decision point: this is a mechanic job and not a small one on most cars — the matrix sits behind the dashboard, so labour dominates the bill; get the diagnosis confirmed before authorising the strip-down. Meanwhile: keep the coolant topped up (a leak that empties the system overheats the engine — the cheap fault becomes an engine), use the AC to demist, and ventilate the cabin — coolant vapour isn't something to breathe for months. Don't use radiator stop-leak as a permanent fix; it can block the matrix and narrow passages elsewhere.
A damp patch has appeared on our living room wall, about a metre up from the floor, and the paint is bubbling. The wall is an outside wall. How do I work out where the water is actually coming from?

Map the patch before theorising: its height, shape, and timing are the evidence. Water enters a wall by only a few routes, and the patch's geography discriminates them: (1) rising damp — moisture wicking up from the ground — produces a tide-mark band rarely higher than about a metre, worst at the wall base with salt deposits; your 'metre up' fits, but true rising damp is rarer than the industry suggests; (2) penetrating damp — a defect outside (cracked render, failed pointing, a leaking gutter dripping on that spot) drives rain through; the patch then worsens after rain and sits opposite the defect, at any height; (3) a leaking pipe or radiator inside the wall/floor — constant, weather-independent; (4) condensation — usually corners, behind furniture, with black mould spots rather than bubbling paint.

Discriminating checks: pencil-outline the patch and date it; note growth after rain vs steady growth (rain-linked = penetrating; steady = plumbing). Go outside and inspect that exact wall section: gutters, downpipe joints, cracked render, a soil or path level built up above the internal floor/damp-proof course. Feel and sniff: salts and a horizontal tide line argue rising; mould argues condensation.

Decision point: gutter, render, and ground-level fixes are DIY/builder; repointing and damp-proof work is a builder's job. Before paying for any injected damp-proof course, get the outside defects and plumbing ruled out — most 'rising damp' is one of the cheaper causes wearing a disguise.

We've found a crack in the wall above our living room doorway — it steps diagonally through the plaster and one brick course outside too. Other hairline cracks elsewhere don't worry me, but this one feels different. Is it?

Your instinct is sound: cracks differ, and this one's features are the ones surveyors take seriously. Learn the discriminators: (1) pattern — a diagonal, stepped crack following mortar joints suggests one part of the building moving relative to another (settlement/subsidence), whereas fine straight hairlines in plaster are usually just shrinkage and thermal movement; (2) width — hairline (under 1mm) is cosmetic; a crack you can fit a pencil tip or a credit card edge into (over ~3mm) indicates real movement; (3) it appears on BOTH faces of the wall (inside plaster and outside brickwork at the same place) — yours does, which means it goes through the structure, not just the finish; (4) behaviour over time — is it growing?

What to do now: measure and monitor — photograph it with a ruler against it, mark the ends with pencil and date them, or fit a simple tell-tale (a strip of glass or a crack gauge) across it; re-check monthly. Note associated signs: doors or windows in that area starting to stick, sloping floors.

Decision point: monitoring is yours; diagnosis is a structural engineer's, and if it's active movement, also your buildings insurer's (subsidence is usually an insured event, and they appoint their own engineers). Don't fill it and forget it, and don't let a general builder repoint it closed without an engineer's view — a filled crack erases the evidence and the movement continues unseen.

Several hairline cracks have appeared in the plaster of our new extension, mostly at the corners of rooms and along the ceiling line. The extension was finished four months ago. Should the builder be worried, or us?

Neither, most likely — this is the most predictable cracking in building: new work drying out and settling into itself. Fresh plaster, screed, timber, and blockwork all hold construction moisture and shrink as they dry over the first year; the cracks appear where movement concentrates — internal corners, ceiling-to-wall junctions, around door frames — and they're characteristically hairline (under 1mm), straight or gently following joints, and they stop growing once drying completes. The four-month timing fits perfectly.

Discriminating checks: width with a ruler (hairline = reassuring); pattern (corner and junction cracks = shrinkage; a diagonal stepped crack through brickwork outside = a different conversation); growth — pencil-mark the ends, date them, and check in a month: stable marks mean a finished process.

Decision point: cosmetic filling and redecorating is the whole cure, ideally after the first full heating season when drying is complete — fill too early and the crack may reopen as the last moisture leaves. Escalate to the builder (and if it worsens, a surveyor) only if cracks widen beyond a couple of millimetres, appear stepped through the external brickwork in matching positions, or come with sticking doors and sloping floors — those change the diagnosis from drying to movement.
Our upstairs floorboards squeak loudly in the hallway whenever anyone walks to the bathroom at night. The boards look sound. Why do floors start squeaking, and can it be fixed without lifting them?

A squeak is movement plus friction: a board flexing slightly underfoot and rubbing against a nail, a joist, or its neighbour. Boards that 'look sound' squeak because the fault is in the fixing, not the timber. Causes in order: (1) nails worked loose over years of flexing — the board now rides up and down the nail shank, and the squeak is wood on metal; (2) the board shrinking slightly so it no longer bears evenly on the joist and rocks; (3) a board end joint flexing where it meets the next board over a joist.

Discriminating check: walk the area slowly while someone watches and listens from beside you — squeaks localise precisely; mark the spot and whether the board visibly moves. A squeak directly over a joist line (fixing failure) vs mid-span (flexing board) suggests different fixes.

Fix paths without lifting: from above, drive screws (not nails) through the board into the joist beside the loose nails — find the joist by its existing nail line; screws pull the board down and stay tight. For tongue-and-groove, powdered graphite or talc worked into the joint sometimes silences rubbing temporarily. Decision point: entirely DIY if you mind the golden rule — before screwing into any floor, know where the pipes and cables run under it (they often notch through joists exactly where you'd screw); use screws no longer than board-plus-joist needs and check what's below from any accessible edge. A floor that feels spongy or bouncy, not just squeaky, is different — that's joist condition, and it wants a carpenter/builder to look.
Our bedroom door has started sticking at the top corner this winter — I have to shoulder it. Last summer it closed perfectly. The house is forty years old. Seasonal or structural?

The timing is your strongest evidence, and it points seasonal. Timber doors and frames absorb moisture in winter, swell, and shrink back in summer — a door that sticks in winter and frees in summer, in a forty-year-old house that has presumably done this quietly for decades (perhaps newly noticeable after painting added a layer, or a wetter winter), is almost always humidity, not the house moving. Structural movement doesn't keep a calendar. Causes in order: (1) seasonal swelling of the door/frame, worst at the top corner if the frame's head has any sag or the door was hung with tight clearances; (2) hinge wear or a loose top hinge letting the door drop slightly so the top corner meets the frame — this one is year-round but often first noticed when swelling removes the last clearance; (3) genuine frame movement — last, and it would usually bring cracks and other sticking doors along.

Discriminating checks: look at the hinge screws — a loose top hinge (screws spinning or the leaf gaping) is a five-minute fix with longer screws into the frame. Check the gap around the closed door: even but tight everywhere = swelling; wedge-shaped gap, wide at the bottom and shut at the top = the door has dropped or the frame moved.

Decision point: hinges and a light planing of the swollen edge (in summer, take off less than you think — it shrinks back) are DIY. Escalate to a surveyor only if the sticking arrives with stepped cracks, several doors and windows sticking at once, or a gap pattern that worsens month on month in dry weather — that's movement, not moisture.
There's black mould growing in the corner of our bedroom ceiling and down the external wall, and the wardrobe against that wall smells musty. The wall feels cold. What's feeding the mould?

Mould needs moisture, and on a cold external corner the moisture is almost always condensation: warm indoor air carries water vapour, the corner (where two external walls meet, the coldest surface in the room, made colder by the wardrobe blocking warm air circulation) sits below dew point, and water condenses there daily — the mould is grazing on that film. Causes in order: (1) condensation from high indoor humidity plus a cold bridge at the corner — the wardrobe's role is diagnostic: furniture against external walls creates a still, cold pocket, which is why the mould maps to it; (2) a penetrating leak from a gutter or roof defect above that corner — check the timing against rain; (3) rising damp — essentially impossible at ceiling height, so rule it out by location.

Discriminating checks: does the patch worsen after rainy days specifically (leak) or steadily through cold weather (condensation)? A hygrometer reading persistently above 60-65% RH convicts the air. Pull the wardrobe out: mould concentrated behind it, with the open wall cleaner, is condensation's fingerprint.

Decision point: kill and clean the mould (with proper precautions — mask, ventilation, mould cleaner), move the wardrobe off the wall or leave a gap, run heating more evenly, ventilate after showers/cooking, and consider a dehumidifier — all DIY/household. A builder is needed only if you find a roof/gutter defect feeding it, or if insulation upgrades (the permanent cure for cold bridges) are on the table.
The grout in our shower has gone black in patches and the silicone seal around the bath is peeling away at one corner. Behind the peeling bit the wall feels slightly soft. How far does this go?

In stages — and the soft wall is the part to respect. Black grout is usually surface mould feeding on soap residue in a permanently damp joint: ugly, mostly cosmetic. Peeling silicone is a maintenance failure with a consequence: that corner is now letting shower water behind the bath every time you use it. The soft-feeling wall behind it suggests plasterboard that has been drinking that water — plasterboard loses its strength when wet and stays soft. So the likely stack is: failed seal (cause), water ingress (mechanism), saturated board (damage so far).

Discriminating checks: press around the area — softness confined to a hand-span near the corner is local damage; softness spreading widely, tiles sounding hollow over a big area, or a musty smell in the room below/behind means the water has travelled. Check the ceiling of the room below for staining.

Decision point: resealing is DIY but do it properly — strip ALL the old silicone (it won't bond to new), let the joint dry out for days (stop using that shower if you can), clean with mould killer, and re-seal with sanitary silicone. If the board is soft over more than a small area, that's a tiler/builder: tiles off, rotten board cut out and replaced, then re-seal — sealing over rotten board just hides a growing problem. And if the room below shows a stain, treat it as the leak it is, not a cosmetic issue.
A section of our wooden garden fence leans more after every storm, and one post wobbles in its hole when I push it. The panels are fine. What's actually failing underground?

Fence posts almost never fail in the visible wood first — they fail at and below ground level, where the post sits in a permanently damp zone. Your wobbling post has lost its grip in the ground. Causes in order: (1) rot at the post's base, concentrated at ground level where moisture and oxygen meet — the post may look sound above ground while being mostly compost at the line that matters; prod the base with a screwdriver: if it sinks in softly, that's it; (2) the concrete footing cracked or the post set too shallow, so the whole plug rocks in an enlarged hole — the post itself will prod solid; (3) soil washed out or very soft ground after a wet winter.

Discriminating check: the screwdriver prod test splits rot from footing failure in ten seconds. Also check whether the lean is one post (local failure) or the whole run progressively leaning (ground or wind exposure issue).

Decision point: this is DIY country — a rotted post gets replaced (or, as a legitimate repair, a concrete spur bolted alongside the sound upper post into a new footing). A solid post with a failed footing can be re-set in fresh concrete with a wider hole. No professional needed unless the fence is tall, on a boundary with a drop, or the 'fence' is actually a retaining structure holding back soil — that changes it from carpentry to structure, and a builder should look.

My cordless drill has lost most of its torque — it stalls driving screws it used to sink easily — and the battery drains in half the time. The battery is three years old. Drill dying or battery dying?

The evidence points at the battery, and here's how to be sure before spending. A drill motor rarely fades gradually; batteries do exactly this: as lithium cells age and accumulate cycles, their internal resistance rises, so under heavy load the voltage sags — the drill sees low voltage precisely when it needs torque, and capacity shrinks in parallel (your halved runtime). Both symptoms from one cause. Causes in order: (1) the aged battery pack; (2) worn motor brushes — only if it's a brushed model, and that usually adds sparking and an electrical smell; (3) a failing trigger/electronics module — typically erratic speed, not uniform weakness.

Discriminating checks: if you have a second pack, swap it — full torque restored ends the inquiry. Try the suspect pack in another tool: weak there too convicts the pack. Check the pack's contacts for corrosion or a bent terminal. Note whether torque is worst in the first minute off the charger (a pack that can't hold surface charge is well gone).

Decision point: a replacement pack is a purchase, not a repair — and often costs most of a new drill kit on offer, so price both. Opening battery packs or motor housings isn't worthwhile or safe for lithium packs. If a known-good pack still stalls, the drill itself is done — repair economics rarely favour small-tool motor work.
My bench grinder vibrates badly for the first few seconds after switching on, then settles to a mild hum. One wheel looks slightly chipped at the edge. Should I keep using it?

No — stop using it until the wheel is dealt with. A grinding wheel that vibrates at start-up and has a visible chip is a safety problem, not a performance quirk: grinding wheels are brittle, run at high rim speed, and a damaged or unbalanced wheel can disintegrate, throwing fragments at face height. The start-up vibration pattern fits a wheel out of balance (from the chip, uneven wear, or moisture absorbed unevenly while standing) or a wheel not seated true on its flanges. Causes in order: (1) the chipped/damaged wheel itself; (2) the wheel mounted off-centre or with damaged/missing paper blotter washers; (3) worn bearings — but those usually hum or rumble constantly rather than settling.

What to do: with the grinder unplugged, inspect the wheel fully — any crack or chip means it comes off and is destroyed (break it so nobody else rescues it). A sound wheel can be ring-tested: suspend it on a finger through the bore and tap it with a wooden handle — a clear ring is healthy, a dull thud means a crack even if you can't see one. Remount with clean flanges and blotters, dress the wheel true with a wheel dresser.

Decision point: wheel changing and dressing are normal user maintenance IF you follow the machine's procedure and match the wheel's rated speed to the grinder. If vibration persists with a new, true wheel, the bearings or spindle are at fault — that's a repair shop, and the grinder stays off meanwhile.
My petrol chainsaw starts easily, idles fine, but dies the moment I squeeze the throttle to cut. It worked last season. Fuel is fresh. What chokes it under load?

Starting and idling well but dying on throttle is a fuel-delivery-under-demand story: at idle the engine sips; on throttle it needs full flow, and something can't supply it. Causes in order: (1) a partially blocked carburettor jet or a stiffened carb diaphragm from last season's fuel residues — fresh fuel in the tank doesn't clean varnish already in the carb; (2) a clogged fuel filter in the tank or a blocked tank vent — the vent is a favourite: as fuel is drawn, a vacuum builds in the tank until flow stops; the tell is the engine recovering after a rest (air slowly leaks back in) and a hiss when you open the cap; (3) a blocked spark-arrestor screen in the exhaust, choking the engine as revs rise; (4) an air leak at the carb gasket leaning the mixture out under load.

Discriminating checks: loosen the fuel cap when it dies — a hiss and an immediate restart points at the vent. Check the spark arrestor screen for carbon crust (a wire brush or heat cleans it). Note whether it dies instantly on throttle (starvation/vacuum) or bogs and smokes first (different fault — too rich, or a flooded crankcase).

Decision point: filters, arrestor screens, and tank vents are owner maintenance. Carburettor strip-downs and mixture screws are where most owners make things worse — a small-engine shop's ultrasonic clean and reset is money well spent. Safety line: never run a saw with guards removed to 'test', and if it dies mid-cut unpredictably, that's a reason to stop cutting until it's fixed — a stalling saw tempts dangerous throttle habits.
The extractor fan in our bathroom has got much louder and rattly over the last year, and the bathroom stays steamy far longer than it used to. Two symptoms, one cause?

Probably yes — the fan is moving less air and complaining about it. Causes in order: (1) the fan's blades and housing furred with dust and lint — bathroom fans inhale moist, lint-laden air for years; the build-up unbalances the impeller (rattle) and strangles airflow (steam lingering); (2) the backdraught shutter or the external vent flap stuck partly shut with the same grime, or blocked by an insect nest outside; (3) the motor bearings wearing — the rattle then is dry and mechanical and persists after cleaning.

Discriminating checks: switch off at the isolator, take the cover off (usually clips or one screw) and look — a felted impeller is a confession. Vacuum and wipe the blades and housing clean, check the outside vent flap moves freely, and test again: tissue held at the grille should grip hard. If it now pulls well and runs quieter, it was dirt. If it pulls well but still rattles, the bearings are going.

Decision point: cleaning is squarely DIY and cures the majority. Replacement fans are like-for-like swaps but involve mains wiring in a bathroom — special-location rules apply, so unless you're confident and competent with isolating and testing, that's an electrician's quick job. Don't just live with it: an under-ventilated bathroom is how you get the mould and condensation problems elsewhere.
Our UPVC front door has become hard to lock — I have to lift the door by the handle while turning the key, and it's getting worse month by month. Is the lock failing?

Usually not the lock — the door has dropped slightly on its hinges, so the multipoint locking bolts no longer align with their keeps in the frame; lifting the handle lifts the door back into alignment, which is why your workaround works. The steady worsening fits gradual hinge sag or the door panel settling in its frame, not a lock mechanism failing (locks tend to fail suddenly or feel gritty rather than progressively misaligning). Causes in order: (1) hinge adjustment drifted or hinges wearing — most UPVC doors have adjustable hinges precisely because this happens; (2) the door 'toe-and-heeling' lost — the glass/panel packing that keeps the door square in its frame has shifted; (3) a dropped frame from a loose fixing — less common.

Discriminating checks: look at the gap between door and frame at the top — wider at the lock side than the hinge side confirms the drop. Check whether the bolts slide freely with the door OPEN (operate the handle with the door ajar): smooth operation open but binding closed proves alignment, not mechanism.

Decision point: hinge adjustment with an Allen key is a legitimate DIY job — small turns, checking as you go, and note the original positions. If adjustment runs out or the door is out of square in its frame (toe-and-heeling), that's a glazier/door technician. Don't keep forcing the key: the next failure in that chain is a snapped key or a failed gearbox in the lock, which turns an adjustment visit into a lock replacement.
One corner of our house has guttering that overflows in heavy rain, spilling down the wall, even though I cleared the leaves out last month. The rest of the gutters cope fine. What's left to check?

A gutter that overflows at one corner after being cleared has a short list, and 'cleared of leaves' only eliminated one item on it. Causes in order: (1) the downpipe below that corner is blocked lower down — leaves leave, but a plug of moss, a tennis ball, or silt at a bend or at the shoe will back water up until the gutter overtops at its lowest point, the corner; the gutter can look clean while the pipe is choked; (2) the gutter's fall is wrong on that run — gutters need a slight slope toward the outlet; a sagging bracket reverses it, ponding water that spills at the corner in heavy flow; (3) the corner joint's seal has failed and what looks like overflow is partly a leak — check in moderate rain: a leak drips steadily from the joint even at low flow, while true overflow only happens at peak.

Discriminating checks: in the next heavy rain (or with a hose in the gutter), watch where the water actually exits — over the top edge (capacity/fall/blockage downstream) vs through the joint (seal). Rod or flush the downpipe from the bottom up, and sight along the gutter for a sag between brackets.

Decision point: rodding a downpipe, resealing a joint with gutter sealant, and adding or repositioning a bracket are ladder-work DIY — with proper ladder care, and never over-reach. If the downpipe drains into a blocked soakaway or drain underground, that becomes a drainage job for a builder/drainage contractor.

The wooden floor in our front room has started to feel bouncy in the middle, and a bookcase against the wall now rattles when someone walks past. The floor was solid when we moved in six years ago. What can make a floor lose its stiffness?

A floor that gains bounce over years is telling you its support has changed — joists don't soften without a cause. In order: (1) joist ends rotting where they sit in the external wall pockets — damp at the wall base rots the bearing ends, the joist loses support and flexes; the front room's external wall is the prime suspect location; (2) a joist cracked or notched — often by a plumber or electrician cutting deep notches for pipes/cables in the middle of the span (illegal placement, common in practice); (3) the subfloor void's ventilation blocked (air bricks covered by raised soil, decking, or a new drive) — the whole underfloor gets damp, and rot and woodworm follow; (4) woodworm or fungal attack weakening joists from within — look for flight holes and frass (fine dust).

Discriminating checks: get under the floor if there's any access (a hatch, a lifted board at the edge) with a torch and a screwdriver: prod joist ends — soft and fibrous is rot; look for notches mid-span; check the air bricks outside are clear. From above, map the bounce: localised to one joist bay vs the whole room.

Decision point: investigation from above and clearing air bricks are yours. Everything structural under a floor is builder/carpenter territory, and if you find active rot or a cracked joist, treat it as prompt work — floors fail gradually then suddenly. Don't just add a rug and a heavier bookcase; the bounce is a measurement, and it's getting worse.

We found a horizontal crack running along the mortar line of our garden retaining wall, and the wall now leans noticeably toward the garden — it holds back about a metre of soil. It's moved maybe two centimetres this year. How do I judge this?

Judge it as a structure that is failing slowly, and treat it with more respect than a garden wall usually gets — a retaining wall holds back real weight, and a metre of saturated soil is tonnes of lateral load. The horizontal crack along a mortar bed plus progressive lean is the classic failure mode: water pressure builds behind the wall (especially if there are no drainage/weep holes, or they're blocked), the soil pushes, and the wall rotates outward at the base or slides on a bed joint. Two centimetres in a year is active movement, not historic settlement.

What to check, from the safe side only: are there weep holes at the base, and are they blocked? Is the ground behind the wall waterlogged, with downpipes or a slope draining toward it? Is the crack wider at one end (rotation) and is any section bulging rather than leaning evenly? Photograph and measure the lean against a fixed reference monthly.

What NOT to do: don't dig out behind the wall to 'relieve pressure' — excavating the retained side can trigger the collapse you're avoiding; don't stand below it during or after heavy rain, when soil load peaks; keep children from playing at its base.

Decision point: this is a structural engineer or an experienced retaining-wall builder, promptly — the repair is usually rebuild with proper drainage (weep holes, gravel backfill, a land drain) rather than patching, because the cause is water, and mortar can't argue with it. If the lean accelerates, the crack opens visibly after rain, or sections start to drop out, cordon it off and treat it as urgent.
